title: Idylls
text:
1. Thyrsis, or the Song
Thyrsis
Sweet is the whispering music of that pine, goatherd,
beside the springs, and sweet your own piping too;
after Pan you will carry off the second prize.
If he takes the horned he-goat, the she-goat is yours;
but if he takes the she-goat for his prize, the kid
falls to you—and kid's flesh is good, until you milk her.
Goatherd
Sweeter, shepherd, is your song than the splashing
of that water that streams down from the rock above.
If the Muses carry off the ewe as their gift,
you shall win the stall-fed lamb as your prize; but if it please them
to take the lamb, then you shall lead away the ewe instead.
Thyrsis
Will you, by the Nymphs—will you, goatherd, sit here
upon this sloping hillside among the tamarisks
and pipe? Meanwhile I will tend the goats in this place.
Goatherd
It is not lawful, shepherd, not at noon, not lawful for us
to pipe. It is Pan we fear; for at this hour he rests,
worn out from the hunt; and he is bitter,
and the sharp gall sits always at his nostrils.
But you, Thyrsis, who used to sing the sorrows of Daphnis
and reached the heights of the pastoral Muse—
come, let us sit here beneath the elm, facing Priapus
and the springs of the Nymphs, where the herdsmen's
seat is, and the oaks. And if you sing
as once you sang when you contended with Chromis of Libya,
I will give you a goat that bears twins, to milk three times,
who though she has two kids yields milk besides for two pails;
and a deep ivy-cup, washed over with sweet wax,
two-handled, newly made, still smelling of the knife.
Around its lips above twists curling ivy,
ivy dusted with golden helichryse; and along it
the tendril winds, glorying in its saffron fruit.
Within is fashioned a woman, such a marvel as the gods could make,
decked with robe and headband. Beside her are men
with beautiful long hair, contending in turn,
one from one side, one from the other, with their words. But these do not touch her heart;
now she glances at this one, laughing,
now she casts her thought toward the other. And they, worn with love,
their eyes long hollow with weariness, labor in vain.
Beyond these is fashioned an old fisherman and a rugged
rock, on which the old man eagerly hauls
a great net for the cast, like a man straining hard.
You would say he was fishing with all the strength of his limbs;
so the sinews stand swollen everywhere about his neck,
gray-haired though he is, and his strength is worthy of youth.
A little way off from the sea-worn old man
is a vineyard heavy with fine clusters reddening,
which a small boy guards, sitting
on the dry stone wall; and about him two foxes—
one ranges along the rows, plundering the ripe grapes,
the other brings all her cunning to bear upon his satchel,
and vows she will not let the child be until
she has set him down to breakfast on dry bread.
But he is plaiting a pretty cricket-cage of asphodel,
fitting it to a reed; and he cares neither for his satchel
nor for the vines so much as he delights in his weaving.
All round the cup is spread the soft acanthus;
an Aeolian wonder, a marvel to amaze your heart.
For this I gave a goat to the Calydonian ferryman
as its price, and a great cheese of white milk;
and never yet has it touched my lips, but still it lies
unstained. With this I would gladly please you,
if you, my friend, will sing me that lovely song.
And I am not mocking you. Come, good man; for your singing
you will hardly keep against the day Hades makes all forget.
Thyrsis
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.

title: Idylls
text:
This is Thyrsis of Etna, and sweet is the voice of Thyrsis.
Where were you when Daphnis was wasting, where were you, Nymphs?
In the fair vales of Peneios, or on Pindos?
For you held not the great stream of the river Anapos,
nor the peak of Etna, nor the holy water of Acis.
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
For him the jackals howled, for him the wolves,
for him the lion out of the wood wept at his death.
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
Many cattle stood about his feet, and many bulls,
and many heifers and calves bewailed him.
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
Hermes came first from the mountain, and said: Daphnis,
who wears you out? For whom, good man, is so great a longing?
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
The cowherds came, the shepherds came, the goatherds came;
all asked what ailed him. Priapus came
and said: Poor Daphnis, why do you waste away, while the girl
goes wandering on foot by every spring, through every grove—
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song—
seeking you? Ah, you are a luckless lover and helpless.
A cowherd you were called, but now you are like a goatherd.
For the goatherd, when he sees the she-goats being mounted,
melts in his eyes, that he himself was not born a he-goat.
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
And you too, when you see the girls laughing,
melt in your eyes, that you do not dance among them.
To these the cowherd answered nothing, but bore
his own bitter love, and bore it to the end of his doom.
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
But the sweet Cyprian came too, laughing,
laughing in secret, yet keeping heavy wrath in her heart,
and said: You boasted, Daphnis, that you would throw Love;
but have you not yourself been thrown by cruel Love?
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
And to her Daphnis answered: Heavy Cyprian,
Cyprian the spiteful, Cyprian hateful to mortals;
already you think the sun has wholly set for me;
but Daphnis, even in Hades, will be a bitter grief to Love.
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
Is it not said the cowherd—go to Ida,
go to Anchises. There are oaks, there is galingale;
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
And Adonis is in his prime, for he too herds his sheep,
and shoots the hares, and hunts all the wild beasts.
Begin, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
Again, may you stand and face Diomedes near at hand,
and say: I conquered Daphnis the cowherd—but fight with me.
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
O wolves, O jackals, O bears denned in the mountains,
farewell. I, Daphnis the cowherd, am no more among the woods,
no more among the thickets, the groves. Farewell, Arethusa,
and you rivers, that pour your fair water down Thymbris.
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
I am that Daphnis who pastured my cattle here,
Daphnis who watered the bulls and the calves here.
Begin again, dear Muses, begin the pastoral song.
O Pan, Pan, whether you are on the long ridges of Lycaeus,
or whether you range over great Maenalus, come to the island
of Sicily, and leave the steep mound and tomb
of Helice, that of Lycaon's son, admired even by the blessed.
Cease, dear Muses, come, cease the pastoral song.
Come, lord, and take this honey-breathing pipe,
a fair one of compacted wax, curved about the lip.
For I am now being dragged by love down to Hades.
Cease, dear Muses, come, cease the pastoral song.
Now bear violets, you brambles, bear them, you thorns,
and let the fair narcissus bloom upon the junipers;

title: Idylls
text:
let all be changed, since Daphnis dies; let the stag drag the hounds,
and from the hills let owls cry out to nightingales.
Cease, dear Muses, come, cease the pastoral song.
So much he said, and ceased; and Aphrodite
wished to raise him up; but all the thread was spent
from the Fates, and Daphnis went to the stream. The eddy washed over
the man dear to the Muses, the man not hated by the Nymphs.
Cease, dear Muses, come, cease the pastoral song.
And you, give me the goat and the cup, that I may milk her
and pour a libation to the Muses. Farewell, again and again, Muses,
farewell; and I will sing for you a sweeter song hereafter.
Goatherd
May your fair mouth, Thyrsis, be filled with honey,
filled with honeycomb, and may you eat the sweet fig
of Aegilus, since you sing better than the cicada.
Look, here is the cup; mark, friend, how sweet it smells;
you will think it has been washed at the springs of the Hours.
Come here, Cissaetha; and you, milk her. And you she-goats,
do not frisk now, or the he-goat will rise upon you.
2. The Sorceresses
Where are my bay-leaves? Bring them, Thestylis; where are the charms?
Wreathe the bowl with crimson wool of a sheep,
that I may bind by sacrifice the cruel man I love,
who, wretch that he is, has not come to me these twelve days,
and does not even know whether I am dead or alive.
Nor has he knocked, the heartless one, at my door. Ah, surely Love
has gone off elsewhere, taking his fickle heart, and Aphrodite too.
Tomorrow I will go to the wrestling-school of Timagetus
to see him, and reproach him for the way he treats me.
But now I will bind him with burnt offerings. Yet, Moon,
shine fair; for to you I will softly sing, divinity,
and to Hecate of the underworld, before whom even the dogs tremble
as she comes over the graves of the dead and the black blood.
Hail, dread Hecate, and to the end stand by me,
and make these drugs no weaker than those of Circe,
or of Medea, or of golden-haired Perimede.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
First the barley-meal melts in the fire. Now scatter it,
Thestylis. Poor fool, where have your wits flown to?
Am I now even to you, you wretch, a thing to mock?
Scatter it, and say these words: I scatter the bones of Delphis.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
Delphis has grieved me; and against Delphis I burn
this bay; and as it crackles loudly when it catches fire,
and suddenly is kindled, and we see not even its ash,
so may the flesh of Delphis too be turned to ash in the flame.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
As I melt this wax with the god's help,
so at once may Delphis of Myndus melt with love.
And as this brazen wheel turns by Aphrodite's power,
so may that man turn restlessly about my doors.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
Now I burn the bran. And you, Artemis, who can move
even the adamant in Hades, and whatever else stands fast—
Thestylis, the dogs are howling for us through the town.
The goddess is at the crossroads. Strike the bronze, quickly.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
See, the sea is silent, and the winds are silent;
but the anguish within my breast is not silent,
for I am all on fire for him, who has made me, poor wretch,
no true wife, but vile and no maiden any more.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
Three times I pour libation, and three times, lady, I say this:
whether it is a woman that lies beside him, or a man,
may he forget them as utterly as they say once Theseus
forgot fair-haired Ariadne on Dia.

title: Idylls
text:
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
There is a plant called horse-madness among the Arcadians, and for it
all the colts and swift mares run wild upon the hills.
So may I see Delphis too, and may he come to this house
like a madman, hurrying from the bright wrestling-school.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
This fringe Delphis lost from his cloak,
which I now pluck apart and cast into the fierce fire.
Alas, cruel Love, why have you fastened on me and drunk
all the black blood from my flesh, like a marsh leech?
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
Tomorrow I will grind a lizard and bring him an evil draught.
But now, Thestylis, take these herbs and smear them
on the lintel of his door above, while it is still night,
and say, spitting as you go: I knead the bones of Delphis.
Iynx, draw that man, my lover, to my house.
Now, being alone, from what shall I begin to weep for my love?
Where shall I start? Who brought this evil upon me?
Anaxo, daughter of Eubulus, went as basket-bearer for us
to the grove of Artemis, around whom that day many other
wild beasts were led in procession in a circle, and among them a lioness.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And Theumaridas' Thracian nurse, that blessed woman,
who lived close by my door, begged and entreated me
to come and watch the procession; and I, ill-fated,
went with her, trailing a fine linen gown,
and wrapped about me the shawl of Clearista.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And already at the middle of the highway, where Lycon's house stands,
I saw Delphis and Eudamippus walking together.
Their beards were yellower than helichryse,
and their breasts gleamed far brighter than you, Moon,
as men just come from the fair labor of the gymnasium.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And as I saw, so I went mad, so my heart was set ablaze,
ill-fated that I am; and my beauty wasted away, and I gave no thought
to that procession, nor did I know how I came home again;
but a parching fever shook me to pieces,
and I lay on my couch ten days and ten nights.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And my skin often became the color of dye-weed,
and all the hair fell from my head, and there was nothing left
but bones and skin. And to whose house did I not go,
or what old woman's home did I leave unvisited, who knew spells?
But there was no easing of it; and time sped fleeting on.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And so I told my slave-girl the truth:
Come, Thestylis, find me some remedy for my cruel sickness.
The man of Myndus possesses me wholly, wretched as I am; but go
and watch by the wrestling-school of Timagetus;
for there he haunts, and there it pleases him to sit.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And when you find him alone, nod to him quietly,
and say Simaetha calls you, and lead him here.
So I spoke; and she went and brought the sleek-skinned Delphis
to my house; and I, when I marked him
just now crossing my threshold with a light step—
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came—
I grew all colder than snow, and on my forehead
the sweat poured down like the moist dew,
nor could I utter a sound, not even as much as children
whimper in their sleep, calling on their dear mother;
but I stiffened all over like a doll, fair body and all.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And when the loveless man looked at me, fixing his eyes on the ground,
he sat on the couch, and sitting he spoke these words:
Truly, Simaetha, by just so much have you outrun me

title: Idylls
text:
as I once, the other day, outran the graceful Philinus in the race,
by calling me to this house of yours before I came to you myself.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
For I would have come—yes, by sweet Love I would have come—
with two or three friends, as soon as it was night,
keeping apples of Dionysus in my bosom,
and on my head white poplar, the holy shoot of Heracles,
twined all about with purple ribbons.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And if you had received me, that would have been welcome; for I am called
nimble and handsome among all the young men;
and I would have slept content, had I but kissed your fair mouth.
But if you had thrust me away, and the door were barred with a bolt,
then surely axes and torches would have come against you.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
But now I said I owed thanks first to the Cyprian,
and after the Cyprian to you, who, woman, snatched me second from the fire
by calling me to this house of yours,
half-burned as I was; for Love, indeed, often kindles
a blaze fiercer than Hephaestus of Lipara.
Consider, lady Moon, whence my love came.
And with his cruel frenzies he scares the maiden from her chamber
and the bride, leaving the bed still warm
with her husband. So he spoke; and I, too quick to believe,
took his hand and drew him down upon the soft couch.
And quickly flesh ripened upon flesh, and our faces
grew warmer than before, and we whispered sweetly;
and—that I may not chatter long to you, dear Moon—
the greatest things were done, and we both came to our desire.
And he found no fault with me, nor I with him,
until yesterday. But there came to me the mother
of Philista, the flute-girl, and of Melixo,
today, just when the horses were running up the sky
bearing rosy-armed Dawn from Ocean.
And she told me, among much else, that Delphis is in love,
and whether it is desire for a woman or a man that holds him
she said she did not know for certain, but only this: that ever for Love
he poured a toast of unmixed wine, and in the end went off in haste,
and said he would deck that house with garlands.
This the stranger-woman told me; and it is true;
for indeed he used to come to me three and four times a day,
and often left his Dorian oil-flask with me;
but now it is twelve days since I have even set eyes on him.
Has he not some other delight, and forgotten me?
Now I will bind him with these love-charms; but if he still
grieves me, by the Fates he shall knock at the gate of Hades.
Such evil drugs, I tell you, I keep for him in my chest,
learned, mistress, from an Assyrian stranger.
But you, fare well, and turn your steeds toward Ocean,
lady; and I will bear my pain as I have endured it.
Farewell, bright-faced Moon, and farewell, you other
stars, attendants on the wheel of quiet Night.
3. The Serenade
I go a-courting to Amaryllis, while my goats
graze on the hill, and Tityrus drives them.
Tityrus, my well-beloved, pasture the goats,
and lead them to the spring, Tityrus, and the Libyan
tawny he-goat—watch him, lest he butt you.
O lovely Amaryllis, why do you no longer peep
from this cave and call me, your darling? Do you hate me?
Do I look snub-nosed to you, close at hand,
nymph, and with too long a chin? You will make me hang myself.
See, here I bring ten apples; I plucked them from the place
where you bade me pluck them; and tomorrow I will bring you more.
Look, look at my heart-grieving sorrow. Would that I were
the humming bee, and might come into your cave,
slipping through the ivy and the fern that hide you.

title: Idylls
text:
Now I know Love; a heavy god he is; truly at a lioness's
teat he sucked, and his mother reared him in the woodland,
he who smolders me and pierces me to the very bone.
O you who look so lovely, but are all stone; O dark-browed
nymph, embrace me, your goatherd, that I may kiss you.
Even in empty kisses there is a sweet delight.
You will make me tear to little pieces, this instant,
the wreath of ivy that I keep for you, dear Amaryllis,
woven with rosebuds and fragrant celery.—
Ah me, what shall I suffer? What, poor wretch? Will you not listen?—
I will strip off my goatskin and leap into the waves yonder,
where Olpis the fisherman watches for the tunny;
and even if I die, at least that will be sweet to you.
I learned the other day, when, thinking of you, I asked whether you love me,
and the love-in-absence, the love-leaf, did not stick and crackle,
but withered idly there upon my smooth forearm.
And Paraebatis, the country sieve-diviner, spoke truth,
she who the other day was gleaning herbs, when she said that I
am wholly set on you, while you make no account of me.
Truly I keep for you a white she-goat that bears twins,
which dark-skinned Mermnon's hired girl also begs of me,
and I will give her to her, since you grow so coy with me.
My right eye twitches. Shall I then see her?
I will lean here against this pine and sing,
and perhaps she will look on me, since she is not of adamant.
When Hippomenes desired to wed the maiden,
he took apples in his hands and ran the race; and Atalanta,
as she saw, so she went mad, so she leapt into deep love.
The seer Melampus too led the herd from Othrys
to Pylos; and so the lovely mother of wise Alphesiboea
was laid in the arms of Bias.
And did not Adonis, pasturing his sheep upon the hills,
drive fair Cytherea to such a height of madness
that not even in death does she lay him from her breast?
I envy Endymion, who sleeps the changeless sleep;
I envy, dear woman, Iasion,
who won such joys as you who are profane shall never learn.
My head aches, but you do not care. I sing no more;
I will lie where I fall, and let the wolves devour me here.
May that be sweet as honey to you, down your throat.
4. The Herdsmen: Battus and Corydon
Battus
Tell me, Corydon, whose are the cattle? Are they Philondas'?
Corydon
No, Aegon's; he gave them to me to pasture.
Battus
And do you somewhere milk them all on the sly at evening?
Corydon
No, the old man puts the calves to suck and keeps an eye on me.
Battus
And the cowherd himself—to what land has he vanished and gone?
Corydon
Have you not heard? Milon took him off to the Alpheus.
Battus
And when did that man ever set eyes on oil for wrestling?
Corydon
They say he rivals Heracles in might and strength.
Battus
And my mother said I was a better man than Polydeuces.
Corydon
And off he went, with his mattock and twenty sheep from here.
Battus
Milon could persuade the very wolves to run mad on the spot.
Corydon
And these heifers, lowing, long for him.
Battus
Poor wretches they are, to have found so bad a herdsman.
Corydon
Poor wretches indeed, and they no longer care to graze.
Battus
Why, of that calf there nothing is left
but the bones. Does it feed on dew, like the cicada?
Corydon
No, by Earth; but at times I pasture her on the Aesarus
and give her a fine bundle of soft hay,
and at times she frisks about deep-shaded Latymnum.
Battus
Lean too is that red bull. May the people, the deme,
the sons of Lampriadas, get just such a one when they sacrifice
to Hera; for an ill-favored lot the deme is.

title: Idylls
text:
Corydon
And yet he is driven to the Salt-Lake, and to Physcus' land,
and to the Neaethus, where all fair things grow,
goat-grass and fleabane and sweet-smelling balm.
Battus
Alas, alas, the cattle too will go, poor Aegon,
down to Hades, since you also fell in love with a sorry victory,
and the pipe you once fashioned is mottled over with mold.
Corydon
Not that, no, by the Nymphs; for setting off to Pisa
he left it me as a gift; and I am something of a player,
and well I strike up the airs of Glauce, and well those of Pyrrhus.
I praise Croton—a fair city—and Zacynthus,
and the eastward-facing Lacinium, where the boxer
Aegon ate up eighty loaves single-handed.
There too he caught the bull on the mountain by its hoof
and led it down, and gave it to Amaryllis; and the women
cried out long and loud, and the cowherd laughed aloud.
Battus
O gracious Amaryllis, you alone, though dead,
we will not forget. As dear as my goats to me, so dear, is your dying.
Alas for the harsh fate that has been allotted me.
Corydon
Take heart, dear Battus; perhaps tomorrow will be better.
The living have hopes, only the dead are without hope.
And Zeus is at one time clear, at another sends rain.
Battus
I take heart. Drive the calves down below; for the wretches
are nibbling the olive-shoot. Get on there, Whitey.
Corydon
Get on, Cymaetha, to the hill. Do you not hear?
I will come, by Pan, and give you a sorry end at once,
if you do not move off from here. Look, here she creeps back again.
Would that I had my crooked throwing-stick, to strike you.
Battus
Look at me, Corydon, for Zeus' sake; for the thorn
has just now pricked me here under the ankle. How deep
these spindle-thistles are. Curse the heifer;
I was pricked gaping after her. Do you see it?
Corydon
Yes, yes, I have it with my nails; here it is.
Battus
How small the wound is, and how great a man it masters.
Corydon
When you go up the hill, do not go barefoot, Battus;
for on the hill the brambles and the thorn-bushes flourish.
Battus
Tell me, Corydon, does the old man still pursue
that dark-browed little love of his, that he was once smitten with?
Corydon
Still indeed, poor fool; only the other day, coming upon him,
I caught him at it hard by the fold while he was about his business.
Battus
Well done, you old lecher. Truly your breed rivals
the little Satyrs, or the spindle-shanked Pans, at close quarters.
5. The Singing-Match: Comatas and Lacon
Comatas
My goats, flee that fellow there, the shepherd of Sibyrtas,
Lacon; he stole my fleece yesterday.
Lacon
Away from the spring! Hsst, lambs. Do you not see
Comatas, who stole my pipe the other day?
Comatas
What pipe? When did you, Sibyrtas' slave,
ever own a pipe? Why are you not content,
along with Corydon, to toot on a whistle of straw?
Lacon
The one Lycon gave me, free man that you are. And as for you,
what fleece did Lacon ever make off with and steal? Tell me, Comatas;
your own master Eumaras had nothing even to sleep in.
Comatas
The dappled one Crocylus gave me, when he sacrificed
the goat to the Nymphs; and you, wretch, even then were sick
with envy, and now in the end you have stripped me bare.
Lacon
No, by Pan of the shore himself, Lacon
the son of Calaethis did not strip you of the goatskin, or may I
fling myself, man, in madness off that rock into the Crathis.
Comatas
No, by the very Nymphs of the marsh, good fellow—
and may they be gracious and kindly to me—
Comatas did not slip up and steal your pipe.
Lacon
If I were to believe you, may I take on the sorrows of Daphnis.

title: Idylls
text:
But come, if you care to stake a kid—it is no great
matter—then I will sing against you until you give up.
Comatas
A pig once vied with Athena. There, the kid
is laid down; come now, you too stake the well-fed lamb.
Lacon
And how, you fox, shall this be even between us?
Who shears hair instead of wool? Who, with a good
first-bearing she-goat at hand, would choose to milk a vile bitch?
Comatas
A man who feels sure, as you do, of beating his neighbor—
a buzzing wasp matched against a cicada. But since the kid
is no fair match for you, here is this he-goat. Sing.
Lacon
No hurry; you are not on fire. You will sing more sweetly
sitting here beneath this wild olive and these groves.
Cool water trickles down here; here have sprung up
grass and this bed of leaves, and here the locusts chatter.
Comatas
I am in no hurry; but I am greatly vexed that you dare
look me in the face with level eyes—me, who once,
when you were still a child, taught you. See where favor comes to in the end.
Rear wolf-cubs, rear dogs, and they will eat you.
Lacon
And when did I ever learn or even hear any good thing from you
that I remember? You spiteful, ill-bred little man, just so.
. . .
But come this way, come, and sing your last herdsman's song.
Comatas
I will not come there; here are oaks, here is galingale,
here the bees hum sweetly about their hives;
here are two springs of cool water; on the tree
the birds are chattering; and the shade is nothing like
the shade by you; and the pine showers down its cones from above.
Lacon
But you will tread on lambskins and on wool here,
if you come, softer than sleep; whereas your goatskins
beside you smell ranker than you yourself smell.
And I will set up a great bowl of white milk
for the Nymphs, and set up another of sweet oil.
Comatas
But if you come, you will tread here on soft fern
and flowering pennyroyal; and under you will lie goatskins
four times softer than the lambskins beside you.
And I will set up eight pails of milk for Pan,
and eight bowls full of combs heavy with honey.
Lacon
There where you are, sing against me, and there make your herdsman's song;
tread your own ground and keep your oaks. But who shall judge
between us? If only the cowherd Lycopas would come this way.
Comatas
I have no need of him; but the man,
if you like, the woodcutter, we will call—he is cutting
those heath-bushes there beside you for firewood; it is Morson.
Lacon
Let us call him.
Comatas
You call him.
Lacon
Come here, stranger, listen a moment;
come this way; for we are contending which is the better
singer of herdsman's songs. And you, friend Morson, neither judge
me with favor, nor yet do this man any favor.
Comatas
Yes, by the Nymphs, dear Morson, neither give Comatas
the more, nor yet show favor to this fellow here.
This flock here belongs to Sibyrtas of Thurii,
and the goats you see, friend, are Eumaras' of Sybaris.
Lacon
Did anyone ask you, for Zeus' sake, whether the flock
is Sibyrtas' or mine, you scoundrel? How you chatter.
Comatas
My good man, I speak everything truthfully
and make no boast; but you are far too fond of jeering.
Lacon
Come, say what you have to say, and let the stranger go
home alive again. O Healer, what a chatterbox you were, Comatas.
Comatas
The Muses love me far more than the singer
Daphnis; and only the other day I sacrificed two kids to them.
Lacon
Apollo too loves me greatly, and a fine ram
I am rearing for him; and the Carnea are even now at hand.
Comatas
I milk goats that bear twins, all but two of those left;

title: Idylls
text:
and the girl, looking on, says, Poor wretch, do you milk all alone?
Lacon
Ah, ah, Lacon fills near twenty baskets
with cheese, and tumbles his boy among the flowers.
Comatas
And Clearista pelts the goatherd with apples
as he drives the goats past, and whistles sweetly after him.
Lacon
And me too the smooth-cheeked Cratidas, coming to meet me,
the shepherd, drives wild; and his sleek hair tosses about his neck.
Comatas
But the dog-rose and the anemone are not to be compared
to roses, whose beds grow along the garden walls.
Lacon
Nor are wild crab-apples to be matched with acorns: the one
has a sorry rind from the holm-oak, the others are honey-sweet.
Comatas
And I shall give the maiden a wood-pigeon presently,
taking it down from the juniper; for there it roosts.
Lacon
But I, when I shear the ewe, will give Cratidas himself
soft wool for a cloak, of my own free gift.
Comatas
Hsst, away from the wild olive, you bleating things; graze here,
on this sloping hillside among the tamarisks.
Lacon
Away from the oak, you, Conarus, and Cinaetha;
graze over here toward the east, where Phalarus does.
Comatas
I have a milk-pail of cypress-wood, and a bowl,
the work of Praxiteles; and I keep these for the girl.
Lacon
And I have a flock-loving dog that throttles wolves,
which I give to my boy to chase all the wild beasts.
Comatas
Locusts that leap over our fence,
do not ravage my vines; for they are young.
Lacon
Cicadas, see how I provoke the goatherd;
just so, I suppose, do you provoke the reapers.
Comatas
I hate the bushy-tailed foxes, that come every evening
to Micon's vines and plunder the grapes.
Lacon
And I too hate the beetles, that devour Philondas'
figs and are borne off downwind.
Comatas
Do you not remember, when I had you at my mercy, and you, grinning,
wriggled prettily and clung to that oak there?
Lacon
That I do not remember; but the time when Eumaras
bound you here and gave you a fine thrashing, that I do know.
Comatas
Now someone is growing bitter, Morson; do you not see?
Go and pull squills from an old woman's grave at once.
Lacon
And I too am nettling someone, Morson; you see it too.
Go and dig the cyclamen there beside the Hales.
Comatas
May Himera flow with milk instead of water; and you, Crathis,
run purple with wine, and may your reeds bear fruit.
Lacon
May the Sybaris spring flow with honey for me, and at dawn
let the girl dip honeycombs, not water, in her pitcher.
Comatas
My goats feed on clover and goat-grass,
and tread the lentisk, and lie among the arbutus.
Lacon
For my ewes the sweet balm is at hand
to feed on, and much rock-rose blooms like roses.
Comatas
I do not love Alcippa, because the other day she did not kiss me,
taking me by the ears, when I gave her the wood-pigeon.
Lacon
But I love Eumedes greatly; for when I gave him
my pipe, he kissed me, a fine kiss and a long one.
Comatas
It is not right, Lacon, for jays to vie with the nightingale,
nor hoopoes with swans; but you, poor wretch, are quarrelsome.
Morson
I bid the shepherd cease. And to you, Comatas,
Morson gives the lamb; and you, when you have sacrificed
to the Nymphs, send Morson a fine portion of meat at once.
Comatas
I will send it, by Pan. Now snort, all my herd
of young goats; for see how loud I will laugh
over Lacon the shepherd, now that at last
I have won the lamb; I will leap to the sky for joy.
My horned goats, take heart; tomorrow I will bathe
you all in the waters of the Sybaris lake.
You there, Whitey, the butter, if you mount any
of the goats, I will geld you before I have made fair offering

title: Idylls
text:
of the lamb to the Nymphs. There he goes again. But may I become
Melanthius instead of Comatas, if I do not geld you.

title: Idylls
text:
6. The Singing-Match: Damoetas and Daphnis
Damoetas and Daphnis the cowherd once drove their herd
together into one place, Aratus; and one of them
was red-haired, the other half-bearded; and sitting both by a spring
at midday in the summer, they sang in this way.
Daphnis began first, for it was he who first challenged.
Galatea pelts your flock, Polyphemus,
with apples, calling you a laggard in love, a goatherd;
and you do not even look at her, poor wretch, poor wretch, but sit
piping sweetly. Look, again she pelts the dog,
which follows as guardian of your sheep; and it barks,
gazing toward the sea, and the fair waves show it
softly plashing as it runs along the shore.
Take care, lest she leap upon the girl's legs
as she comes from the sea, and tear her lovely skin.
But she even from there coquets with you, light
as the dry thistledown when the fair summer parches it;
and she flees the one who loves her, and pursues the one who does not,
and moves her last counter on the line; for to a lover,
Polyphemus, things not fair often appear fair.
After him Damoetas struck up and sang as follows.
I saw her, by Pan, when she was pelting the flock,
and she did not escape my notice, no, by this one sweet eye of mine, with which I shall see
to the end; but as for the seer Telemus, who speaks ill words,
let him bear his ill words home, to keep them for his children.
Yet I myself, to tease her in turn, do not look at her,
but say I have some other woman; and she, hearing this,
grows jealous of me, by the Healer, and pines away, and from the sea
she peers out in a frenzy at the caves and at the flocks.
And I hissed the dog to bark at her; for when I loved her,
it would whimper, laying its muzzle against her flank.
Seeing me do this often, perhaps she will send
a messenger. But I will bar my doors, until she swears

title: Idylls
text:
to spread a fair bed for me herself upon this island.
For indeed I am not so ill to look at as they say.
The other day I gazed into the sea, when it was calm,
and fair my beard, and fair my one eye seemed,
so far as I could judge, and the gleam of my teeth
showed whiter than the marble of Paros.
And, lest I be bewitched, I spat three times into my bosom;
for so the old woman Cotyttaris taught me.
Having said so much, Damoetas kissed Daphnis,
and the one gave him a pipe, the other a fine flute.
Damoetas played the flute, and Daphnis the cowherd piped,
and at once the heifers danced upon the soft grass.
But neither was the victor, for they came out unbeaten.
7. The Harvest-Home
There was a time when Eucritus and I were walking from the city
toward the Hales, and a third with us was Amyntas;
for to Demeter, Phrasidamus and Antigenes were keeping
the harvest-feast, two sons of Lycopeus, the best of any noble line
descended from above, from Clytia and from Chalcon himself,
who brought the spring Burina forth at the touch of his foot,
setting his knee firmly against the rock; and beside it
poplars and elms wove a shady grove,
roofed over and leafy with their green foliage.
We had not yet finished half the road, nor had the tomb
of Brasilas come into our sight, when by the favor of the Muses
we met a good wayfarer, a man of Cydonia,
Lycidas by name, a goatherd, nor could anyone
mistake him at a glance, for he looked a goatherd through and through.
For from a shaggy, rough-haired he-goat he had
a tawny skin upon his shoulders, smelling of fresh rennet,
and about his breast an old cloak was girt
with a broad belt, and in his right hand he held
a crooked club of wild olive. And gently, with a grin
and a smiling eye, he spoke to me, and laughter clung to his lip:
Simichidas, where are you dragging your feet at noon,

title: Idylls
text:
when even the lizard sleeps in the dry-stone walls,
and the crested larks of the tombs do not roam abroad?
Are you hurrying to a feast you were bidden to? Or do you leap
to some townsman's wine-press? For as you go, every
stone strikes ringing against your boots and sings.
And I answered him: Dear Lycidas, all men say
you are by far the best of pipers among the herdsmen
and among the reapers. This greatly warms my heart;
and yet in my own mind I hope to be your match.
This journey is to a harvest-feast; for some comrades
are making a banquet to fair-robed Demeter,
offering the first-fruits of their wealth; for with a rich measure
the goddess has filled their threshing-floor with abundant barley.
But come now—the road is common to us, and common too the dawn—
let us make our herdsman's songs; perhaps one will profit the other.
For I too am a clear-voiced mouth of the Muses, and all men call me
the best of singers; but I am not quick to believe,
no, by Earth; for in my own judgment I do not yet outsing
either the noble Sicelidas of Samos or Philitas,
but contend like a frog against the crickets.
So I spoke, on purpose; and the goatherd, with a sweet laugh,
said: I give you this club as a gift, because you are
a sapling shaped by Zeus, all true.
For I greatly hate the builder who tries
to raise a house as high as the peak of Oromedon the mountain,
and those cocks of the Muses who, crowing in rivalry
against the bard of Chios, toil all in vain.
But come, let us quickly begin the herdsman's song,
Simichidas; and I—see, friend, whether you like
this little song that I worked at on the hill the other day.
Lycidas
A fair voyage to Mitylene shall Ageanax have,
both when the south wind drives the wet waves before the Kids at evening,
and when Orion sets his feet upon the ocean,
if only he rescues Lycidas, who is scorched by Aphrodite;

title: Idylls
text:
for hot love for him consumes me.
And the halcyons shall calm the waves and the sea
and the south wind and the east, that stirs the seaweed in the deeps;
the halcyons, of all birds dearest to the gray Nereids,
and to all whose prey is gathered from the sea.
For Ageanax, who seeks a voyage to Mitylene,
may all be seasonable, and may he reach a safe harbor.
And I, on that day, with anise or roses
or with a wreath of white violets about my head,
will draw the Ptelean wine from the bowl,
lying beside the fire, while someone roasts a bean in the embers.
And the couch will be heaped a cubit deep
with fleabane and asphodel and curling celery.
And I will drink at ease, remembering Ageanax,
draining the very cups, pressing my lip to the dregs.
Two shepherds will play the flute for me, one from Acharnae,
one from Lycope; and Tityrus close by will sing
how once Daphnis the cowherd loved Xenea,
and how the mountain grieved about him, and how the oaks lamented him,
those that grow along the banks of the river Himeras,
while he melted like snow under high Haemus
or Athos or Rhodope or the far Caucasus.
And he will sing how once the wide chest received the goatherd,
still living, through the wicked malice of his lord,
and how the snub-nosed bees, coming from the meadow,
fed him in the sweet cedar-chest with soft flowers,
because the Muse poured sweet nectar over his mouth.
O blessed Comatas, these are the joys you knew;
you too were shut into the chest, and you, fed on the bees'
honeycomb, lived out the spring of the year.
Would that you had been counted among the living in my day,
that I might have pastured your fair goats upon the hills,
listening to your voice, while you under the oaks or the pines
lay piping sweetly, godlike Comatas.
When he had said so much he ceased; and after him in turn

title: Idylls
text:
I too spoke thus: Dear Lycidas, many other
fair things have the Nymphs taught me too, as I herded on the hills,
songs that perhaps even rumor has carried to the throne of Zeus;
but this is the best by far of all, with which I will begin
to honor you; only listen, since you are dear to the Muses.
Simichidas
The Loves have sneezed for Simichidas; for the poor wretch
loves Myrto as much as goats love the spring.
But Aratus, dearest of all to that man,
keeps in his heart a longing for a boy. Aristis knows it,
a good man, a great and excellent man, whom not even Phoebus himself
would grudge to sing with his lyre beside the tripods,
how Aratus from a boy has been burned to the bone with love.
For him, Pan, you who have the lovely plain of Homole for your portion,
set the boy unbidden in his dear hands,
whether it is soft Philinus or some other.
And if you do this, dear Pan, then may no Arcadian boys
scourge your sides and shoulders with squills
when there is scant meat at hand;
but if you nod the other way, then may you scratch and bite
yourself all over with your nails, and sleep among the nettles,
and may you be in the mountains of the Edonians at midwinter,
turned toward the river Hebrus, close to the Bear,
and in summer pasture among the farthest Ethiopians
under the rock of the Blemyes, whence the Nile is seen no more.
But you Loves, leaving the sweet stream of Hyetis and Byblis,
and Oecus, the steep seat of golden Dione,
you who are like to ruddy apples,
strike for me with your bows the lovely Philinus,
strike him, since the wretch has no pity on my friend the stranger.
And indeed he is now more overripe than a pear, and the women
say, Alas, Philinus, your fair bloom is dropping away.
Let us no longer keep watch at his doors, Aratus,
nor wear out our feet; but let the cock at dawn,

title: Idylls
text:
crowing, give some other man over to bitter numbness,
and let one man only, good Molon, be throttled at that wrestling-school,
while ease be our care, and an old woman be at hand,
who, spitting, may ward off all that is unlovely.
So much I said; and he, with a sweet laugh
as before, gave me the throwing-stick to be a gift of friendship from the Muses.
And he, turning aside to the left, took the road
to Pyxa; while Eucritus and I, and the fair Amyntichus,
turning to the house of Phrasidamus, lay down
among deep beds of sweet rushes,
rejoicing in the newly stripped vine-leaves.
Many poplars and elms waved above
over our heads; and close by, the holy water
trickled murmuring from the cave of the Nymphs.
In the shady boughs the sun-burnt cicadas
kept their chattering toil; and far off the tree-frog
cried among the thick thorns of the brambles.
The larks and goldfinches sang, the turtle-dove moaned,
and the tawny bees flitted about the springs.
All breathed of rich summer, all breathed of harvest-time.
Pears at our feet, and apples by our sides
rolled in abundance; and the boughs hung down to the ground
weighted with sloes;
and the four-year-old seal was loosed from the wine-jars' mouths.
You Nymphs of Castalia, who hold the peak of Parnassus,
was it ever such a bowl as this that old Chiron
set up for Heracles in the rocky cave of Pholus?
Was it such nectar that prompted that shepherd by the Anapus,
mighty Polyphemus, who hurled mountains at ships,
to dance about the steadings on his feet,
as the draught you then mingled for us, you Nymphs,
beside the altar of Demeter of the threshing-floor? Upon her heap
may I once again plant the great winnowing-fan,
while she smiles, holding sheaves and poppies in both her hands.
8. The Singing-Match: Daphnis and Menalcas
With the graceful Daphnis, as he herded his cattle,

title: Idylls
text:
Menalcas met, pasturing his sheep, they say, on the long hills.
Both of them were red-haired, both still beardless,
both skilled in piping, both in singing.
And Menalcas, looking at Daphnis, was the first to speak:
Daphnis, guardian of the lowing cattle, will you sing against me?
I say I will beat you, singing as long as I choose.
And Daphnis answered him with these words:
Menalcas, shepherd of the woolly sheep, you piper,
you will never beat me, however you may strain at singing.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text: Then do you care to put it to the test? Do you care to set up a prize?

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text: I care to put it to the test; I care to set up a prize.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text: And what shall we stake that would be worthy of us?

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text: I will stake a calf; do you stake a lamb as big as its mother.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
I will never stake a lamb, for my father is harsh,
and my mother too, and they count all the sheep at evening.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text: But what then will you stake? What more shall the winner have?

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
A pipe that I made, a fair one of nine reeds,
set with white wax, even below and even above—
this I will stake; but I will not stake my father's goods.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
Why, I too have a pipe of nine reeds,
set with white wax, even below and even above.
I fitted it together the other day; and I still feel a pain
in this finger, where a reed split and cut me.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text: But who shall judge between us? Who shall hear us?

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
What if we call that goatherd over here,
the one at whose kids the white-spotted dog is barking?
So the boys shouted, and the goatherd came to listen.
The boys sang, and the goatherd was willing to judge.
And first, having drawn the lot, the loud-voiced Menalcas sang,
then Daphnis took up the answering song.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
You glens and rivers, race divine, if ever Menalcas
the piper sang you a song you loved,
graze his ewe-lambs with a good will; and if ever Daphnis
come with his heifers, may he have no less.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
You springs and pastures, sweet growth, if Daphnis
makes music like the nightingales,
fatten this herd of mine; and if Menalcas
brings any here, may he too feed all in plenty, and rejoice.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
Here are the ewes, here the goats that bear twins, here the bees
fill their hives, and here the oaks grow taller,
here the fair Milon sets his feet; but if he goes away,
then dry are both the shepherd and the pastures there.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
Spring everywhere, everywhere the meadows, everywhere with milk
the udders swell, and the young are reared,
wherever the fair girl walks; but if she goes away,
then withered are both the cowherd and his cattle.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
O he-goat, husband of the white she-goats, O depth of the woodland
without end—(O snub-nosed kids, come here to the water)—
for there he is; go, you stub-horned one, and say: Milon,
even Proteus, though a god, pastured his seals.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
May I not have the land of Pelops, nor talents of gold
to possess, nor to outrun the winds;
but under this rock will I sing, holding you in my arms,
watching the flocks graze together, toward the Sicilian sea.

title: Idylls
text: Daphnis

title: Idylls
text:
For the trees winter is a dread evil, for the waters drought,
for the birds the snare, for the wild beasts the net,
for a man the longing for a tender maiden. O father, O Zeus,
I am not the only one to have loved; you too love women.
So the boys sang in answering strains;
and Menalcas led off the last song in this way.
Spare my kids, wolf, spare my mothers,
and do me no wrong, though I am small and tend so many.
O Lampurus, my dog, are you held by so deep a sleep?
You should not sleep deeply when you herd with a boy.
And you, my ewes, do not be slow to feed your fill on the soft
grass; you will not tire, for it will grow again.
Hsst, graze, graze, and fill your udders, all of you,
that the lambs may have part, and part I may lay by in the baskets.
Then Daphnis in his turn struck up clear-voiced to sing:
And me too, the other day, a girl with meeting brows, looking from the cave
as I drove my heifers past, called fair, fair;
but I gave her no answer back, not even a bitter one,
but looking down I went on my own way.
Sweet is the heifer's voice, sweet her breath;
and sweet in summer to lie in the open air by running water.
For the oak the acorns are an ornament, for the apple-tree the apples,
for the cow the calf, for the cowherd the cattle themselves.
So the boys sang, and the goatherd spoke thus:
Sweet is your mouth, Daphnis, and lovely your voice.
Better to hear you singing than to lick honey.
Take the pipes; for you have won in the singing.
And if you are willing to teach me too, who herd goats beside you,
I will give you that hornless goat as your teaching-fee,
who always fills the pail above the brim.
As the boy rejoiced and leaped and clapped his hands,
having won, so might a fawn leap to its mother;
and as the other smoldered and was overturned in his heart with grief,

title: Idylls
text:
so might a bride be grieved when she is wed against her will.
And from that time Daphnis was first among the shepherds,
and, while still in his early youth, he wed the Naiad nymph.
9. The Singing-Match: Daphnis and Menalcas
Daphnis
Sweetly the calf lows, and sweetly the cow,
sweetly the pipe and the cowherd, and sweetly too I sing.
I have a couch of leaves by the cool water, and on it are heaped
the fair hides of white heifers, which all of them
the southwest wind, as they browsed the arbutus, shook down from the crag.
And of the burning summer I take as little heed
as a lover takes of his father's words and his mother's.
So Daphnis sang to me, and so did Menalcas.

title: Idylls
text: Menalcas

title: Idylls
text:
Etna, my mother, I too dwell in a fair cave
among the hollow rocks; and I have such things as appear
in a dream: many sheep, and many she-goats,
whose fleeces lie about my head and at my feet.
In a fire of oak the puddings boil, and dry beech-nuts
roast in the fire when it freezes; and I care no more
for winter than a toothless man cares for nuts when porridge is by.
I clapped my hands for them, and at once gave each a gift,
to Daphnis a club, which my father's field reared for me,
self-grown, such as not even a craftsman could fault,
and to the other a fine spiral whelk-shell, whose flesh I myself
had eaten, watching among the Icarian rocks,
cutting it into five for the five of us; and he blew a blast on the shell.
Hail, pastoral Muses, and bring to light the songs
that once, in those herdsmen's company, I sang;
and may I never raise a blister on my tongue's tip again.
Cicada is dear to cicada, and ant to ant,
and hawks to hawks, but to me the Muse and song.
Of these may all my house be full. For neither sleep
nor sudden spring is sweeter, nor to the bees
their flowers; so dear to me are the Muses. Whomever they look upon
they make glad, and those Circe never harmed with her draught.

title: Idylls
text:
10. The Workmen, or Reapers
Milon
Bucaeus, you laborer, what ails you now, poor wretch?
You can neither drive your swath straight, as you did before,
nor keep pace in the reaping with your neighbor, but fall behind
like a sheep that has hurt its foot on a thorn and lags the flock.
What will you be at evening and from midday on,
you who now, just beginning the furrow, do not bite your way through?
Battus
Milon, you late-reaping man, chip off the unyielding rock,
has it never befallen you to long for someone away?
Milon
Never. What longing has a working man for things outside his work?
Battus
Then it never befell you to lie awake for love?
Milon
And may it never; it is a bad thing to give a dog a taste of tripe.
Battus
But I, Milon, have been in love now near eleven days.
Battus
You draw from a full cask, that is plain; while I have not even vinegar enough.
Battus
And so before my door all is left undug since the sowing.
Milon
And which of the girls is doing you this harm?
Battus
Polybotas' daughter,
who the other day was piping to the reapers at Hippocion's.
Milon
The god has found out the sinner; you have long had what you longed for.
A grasshopper of a girl will lie by you all night.
Battus
You are beginning to mock me; but Wealth is not the only blind one,
so is heedless Love. Do not talk so big.
Milon
I am not talking big; only lay the grain low,
and strike up some love-song for the girl. So you will work
the more pleasantly; and indeed you were once a musical fellow.
Battus
You Pierian Muses, sing with me of the slender
girl; for whatever you touch, goddesses, you make fair.
Lovely Bombyca, all men call you the Syrian,
lean and sunburnt, but I alone call you honey-pale.
The violet too is dark, and the lettered hyacinth,
yet in the garlands they are reckoned first of all.
The goat pursues the clover, the wolf the goat,
the crane the plough, and I am mad for you.
Would that I had all that they say Croesus once possessed;
then we would both stand dedicated, golden, to Aphrodite,
you holding your flutes, and a rose, or an apple too,
and I with new attire and new shoes on both my feet.
Lovely Bombyca, your feet are like knucklebones,
your voice like nightshade; but your ways I have no words to tell.
Milon
How fine the songs the cowherd had been making all unknown to us.
How well he measured out the form of his harmony.
Alas for my beard, that I have grown so vainly.
But hear these too, the lines of godlike Lityerses.
Demeter, rich in fruit and in ears of grain, may this crop
be easy to work and as fruitful as may be.
Bind the sheaves tight, you binders, lest a passer-by
say: These are men of fig-wood, and this hire too is wasted.
Let the cut end of your stubble-rows face
the north wind or the west; so the ear grows full.
Those who thresh the grain should shun the noonday sleep;
at that hour above all the chaff parts best from the straw.
Begin to reap when the lark is rising,
and leave off when it sleeps, and rest in the heat.
Enviable, my boys, is the frog's life; he cares not
for one to pour him drink, for he has it in plenty.
Better, you stingy steward, to boil the lentils thoroughly;
take care you do not cut your hand splitting the cumin too fine.
Such songs men who toil in the sun should sing;
but your starveling love, Bucaeus, is fit to be told
to your mother as she wakes at dawn in her bed.
11. The Cyclops
There is no other remedy for love, Nicias,
no ointment, it seems to me, and no powder,
except the Pierian Muses; a light thing this and sweet

title: Idylls
text:
it proves for men, but not easy to find.
I think you know it well, being a physician,
and beyond others dear to the nine Muses.
So at least the Cyclops who lived among us got through it most easily,
old Polyphemus, when he loved Galatea,
his cheeks and temples just beginning to show a beard.
He loved not with apples, nor with roses, nor with curls,
but with sheer frenzy, and counted all else trifling.
Often his sheep came back of themselves to the fold
from the green pasture, while he, singing of Galatea,
wasted away there upon the weedy shore
from dawn, having the most hateful wound beneath his heart
from the great Cyprian, who had fixed her dart in his liver.
But he found the remedy, and sitting upon a high
rock and looking out to sea, he sang like this.
O white Galatea, why do you spurn the one who loves you?
Whiter to look on than curd, softer than a lamb,
more skittish than a calf, sleeker than the unripe grape.
You come, just so, whenever sweet sleep holds me,
and you go straightway off, as soon as sweet sleep releases me,
and you flee like a sheep that has caught sight of the gray wolf.
I fell in love with you, girl, when first
you came with my mother, wishing to pluck hyacinth leaves
from the hill, and I was your guide upon the way.
And I cannot cease, having once seen you, nor even now
since then; but you do not care, no, by Zeus, not at all.
I know, gracious girl, why you flee;
it is because a shaggy brow stretches over all my forehead,
from one ear to the other, one long unbroken line,
and a single eye is on it, and a broad nose over the lip.
But, such as I am, I pasture a thousand head of cattle,
and from them I draw and drink the best milk;
cheese fails me neither in summer nor in autumn,
nor in the depth of winter; my racks are always overloaded.
And I can pipe as no other Cyclops here can,
singing of you, my dear sweet-apple, and of myself together,
often deep in the night. And I am rearing for you eleven fawns,
all marked with a crescent, and four bear-cubs.
Come to me, then, and you shall lack for nothing,
and leave the gray sea to roar against the shore.
You will pass the night more sweetly with me in the cave.
There are bay-trees there, there slender cypresses,
there is dark ivy, there the vine with its sweet fruit,
there is cool water, which leafy Etna sends me
from her white snow, an ambrosial drink.
Who would choose to have the sea and its waves instead of this?
But if I seem to you too shaggy myself,
I have oak logs and a tireless fire beneath the ashes;
and to be burned by you I would endure even my soul
and this one eye, than which nothing is sweeter to me.
Alas, that my mother did not bear me with gills,
so that I might dive down to you and kiss your hand,
if you would not let me kiss your mouth; and I would bring you white lilies
or the soft poppy with its red petals.
But these come in summer, those in winter,
so that I could not bring you all of them at once.
Now, at least, my girl, now I will learn to swim,
if some stranger sailing here in a ship should come,
that I may know what pleasure you find in dwelling in the deep.
Come out, Galatea, and coming out forget,
as I do now sitting here, to go home again.
Be willing to keep flocks with me, and to milk,
and to set cheese, putting in the sharp rennet.
It is my mother alone who wrongs me, and I blame her;
for she has never once spoken a kind word for me to you,
though she sees me growing thin from day to day.
I will say that my head and both my feet
are throbbing, that she may be grieved, since I too am grieved.

title: Idylls
text:
O Cyclops, Cyclops, where have your wits flown?
If you would go and plait baskets and cut foliage
to bring your lambs, you would surely show far more sense.
Milk the one at hand. Why pursue the one who flees?
You will find another Galatea, perhaps even fairer.
Many girls bid me play with them through the night,
and they all giggle whenever I give them ear;
clearly I too seem to be somebody in the land.
So Polyphemus shepherded his love
by making music, and got through it more easily than if he had paid in gold.
12. The Beloved
You have come, dear boy, with the third night and the dawn?
You have come; and those who long grow old in a single day.
As much as spring is sweeter than winter, as much as the apple
than the sloe, as much as the ewe is more fleecy than her lamb,
as much as a maiden surpasses a thrice-wedded woman,
as much as the fawn is nimbler than the calf, as much as the nightingale
is the most musical in voice of all winged things,
so much have you gladdened me by appearing; and I ran
to your shade like a wayfarer to a beech when the sun is scorching.
Would that the Loves might breathe equally upon us both,
and that we two might become a song to all that come after.
Two godlike men were these among the men of old,
the one the inspirer, as a man of Amyclae would say,
the other again, as the Thessalian would call him, the beloved.
They loved each other with an even yoke. Truly then there were
golden men once more, when the loved one loved in return.
Would that this might be, father, son of Cronos; would that the ageless
immortals might grant that, after two hundred generations,
someone might bring me word, by the path that has no return, to Acheron:
This love of yours and of the gracious beloved
is now on all men's lips, and most of all among the young.
But truly the gods of heaven, who are above these things,
will do as they will; yet I, praising you who are fair,
will raise no false growth of lies above my slender nose.
For even if you bite me, you have at once made it harmless,
and given me twice the joy, and I went off with measure to spare.
You men of Nisaean Megara, foremost at the oar,
may you dwell in happiness, for you honored beyond all others
the Attic stranger Diocles, the lover of boys.
Always about his tomb at the first of spring, gathered together,
the boys contend to carry off the prize of a kiss.
And whoever presses lips most sweetly to lips
goes off to his mother weighed down with garlands.
Happy is he who judges those kisses for the boys.
Surely he calls much upon bright-eyed Ganymede
to give his mouth a touch like the Lydian stone, by which
the money-changers make sure the gold is no base counterfeit.
13. Hylas
Not for us alone, as we used to think,
Nicias, was Love begotten, by whichever of the gods he came as a child.
Not to us first do fair things appear fair,
who are mortal and cannot see the morrow;
but the bronze-hearted son of Amphitryon too,
who withstood the savage lion, loved a boy,
the graceful Hylas, who still wore his hair in a braid;
and he taught him everything, as a father teaches a dear son,
all that he had learned to make himself good and famous;
and never apart from him would he be, neither when midday rose,
nor when white-horsed Dawn ran up to the house of Zeus,
nor when the twittering nestlings looked toward their roost,
their mother fluttering her wings on the smoke-stained rafter,
so that the boy might be trained to his own heart's mind,
and, well drawn on, might turn out a true man at his side.

title: Idylls
text:
But when Jason, son of Aeson, sailed after the golden
fleece, and the chiefs followed him,
chosen out of all the cities, men of some worth,
then the man of much-enduring toil came too to rich Iolcus,
the son of Alcmena, the heroine of Midea,
and with him Hylas went down to the well-benched Argo,
the ship that did not touch the dark Clashing Rocks
but darted clear through—and ran into deep Phasis—
like an eagle, into the great gulf; and from that time they stood fast as reefs.
When the Pleiades are rising, and the upland fields
pasture the young lamb, and the spring has already turned,
then the divine flower of heroes took thought of sailing,
and seating themselves in the hollow Argo
they came to the Hellespont with the south wind blowing on the third day,
and set their mooring within the Propontis, where the oxen
of the Cianians widen the furrows and wear the ploughshares smooth.
Going ashore upon the beach, by their thwarts they made their meal
at evening, and many of them spread one common bed of leaves.
For a meadow lay before them, a great help for couches,
whence they cut sharp sedge and deep galingale.
And golden Hylas went to fetch water for the supper
for Heracles himself and steadfast Telamon,
who being comrades always shared one table,
carrying a bronze pitcher. And soon he saw a spring
in a low-lying place; and about it grew many rushes,
dark celandine and green maidenhair,
and flourishing celery and creeping marsh-grass.
In the midst of the water the Nymphs were forming their dance,
the sleepless Nymphs, dread goddesses to country folk,
Eunica and Malis and Nycheia with the spring in her eyes.
Now the boy was holding out his roomy jar to the water,
eager to dip it, when they all clung to his hand;
for love of the Argive boy had stirred the tender hearts
of all of them; and he fell headlong into the dark water,
all at once, as when a fiery star falls from the sky
all at once, into the sea, and some sailor says to his comrades:
Lighten your tackle, boys; the wind is fair for sailing.
And the Nymphs, holding the boy weeping upon their knees,
soothed him with gentle words.
But the son of Amphitryon, troubled for the boy,
went off, taking his well-bent Maeotian bow
and the club that his right hand always grasped.
Three times he called Hylas, as loud as his deep throat could roar;
three times the boy answered, but his voice came thin
from the water, and though close at hand he seemed very far.
And as when a maned lion, hearing from afar,
a flesh-eating lion in the hills, a fawn's cry,
hastens from his lair to a meal most ready;
so Heracles, among the trackless thorns,
longing for the boy, was driven distracted, and ranged over much ground.
Wretched are lovers; how much he suffered wandering
over mountains and thickets, and all Jason's affairs came second to this.
The ship lay with her tackle aloft, manned by those who were present,
and the demigods at midnight were clearing the sails,
waiting for Heracles. But he went where his feet led him
in his frenzy; for a cruel god gnawed his liver within.
So fairest Hylas is numbered among the blessed;
but the heroes taunted Heracles for deserting the ship,
because he abandoned the thirty-benched Argo,
and on foot came to the Colchians and inhospitable Phasis.
14. The Love of Cynisca, or Thyonichus
Aeschinas
Many greetings to the good Thyonichus.
Thyonichus
And the same to you,
Aeschinas.
Aeschinas
How long it has been.
Thyonichus
Long? But what is your trouble?
Aeschinas
Things go not too well with me, Thyonichus.

title: Idylls
text:
Thyonichus
That is why you are thin,
and this mustache so heavy, and your locks unkempt.
Just such a man came the other day, a Pythagorean,
pale and barefoot; and he said he was an Athenian.
He too was in love, I think—with toasted meal.
Aeschinas
You are forever joking, good fellow; but me the graceful Cynisca
insults; and I shall go mad one day before I know it, by a hair's breadth.
Thyonichus
Such you always are, dear Aeschinas, quietly hot,
wanting everything to your own moment; but tell me, what is the news?
Aeschinas
The Argive, and I, and the Thessalian horse-tamer,
Apis, and Cleunicus the soldier, were drinking
at my place in the country. I had killed two chickens
and a suckling pig, and opened for them a jar of Biblian wine,
fragrant, four years old, almost as fresh as from the press.
Onion, shellfish, snails were brought out. The drinking was pleasant.
And as it went on, we resolved that each man should toast
unmixed to whomever he pleased; only he had to name the name.
We drank as we named, as had been agreed;
but she said nothing, though I was there. What state do you think I was in?
Will you not speak? You have seen a wolf, someone joked. How clever, she said,
and caught fire; you could easily have lit a lamp from her.
There is Lycus—Wolf—there is Lycus, the son of Labas our neighbor,
tall and tender, thought handsome by many.
For him she was melting with that famous love.
And this had come somehow quietly to my ear before;
but I had not looked into it, grown a man for nothing.
By now the four of us were deep in our cups,
and the man of Larisa began to sing my Wolf from the start,
a Thessalian air, with malice; and Cynisca
wept suddenly, more abundantly than a six-year-old girl
weeps by her mother, longing for her lap.
Then I—you know me, Thyonichus—struck her on the cheek
with my fist, and again a second time. She gathered up her gown
and was off and out the quicker. My ruin, do I not please you?
Is another sweeter in your lap? Go and warm some other
dear one. For him your tears flow like apples.
The swallow, having given a morsel to her nestlings under the eaves,
flies swiftly back to gather more food for life;
quicker than that she ran from the soft chair,
straight through the porch and the double doors, where her feet led her.
There is a saying, they tell: the bull went off into the wood.
Twenty; then eight; then nine; then ten more;
today is the eleventh; add two, and it is two months
since we parted. I might be cropped Thracian fashion for all
she knows. Now all is Lycus; for Lycus even the door stands open by night.
But I am worth no man's word, nor counted at all,
a wretched Megarian in the most dishonored rank.
If only I could fall out of love, all would go as it should.
But now, where from? Like the mouse, Thyonichus, they say, I have tasted pitch.
And what the remedy is for a helpless love,
I do not know. Except that Simus, who loved the daughter of Epichalcus,
sailed away and came home cured, a man of my own age.
I too will sail across the sea; no worst of soldiers,
nor first perhaps, but an even, ordinary one.
Thyonichus
I could wish things had gone as you desired, Aeschinas.
But if you are really minded to go abroad,
Ptolemy is the best paymaster a free man could have.
Aeschinas
And in other respects, what kind of man is he?
Thyonichus
Considerate, a lover of the Muses, amorous, the height of charm,
knowing his friend, and still more the man who is not his friend;
giving much to many, refusing none who ask,
as befits a king; though one must not ask on every occasion,

title: Idylls
text:
Aeschinas. So if it suits you to pin
your cloak's end on your right shoulder, and, standing firm on both feet,
to dare to await the bold spearman's charge,
then off with all speed to Egypt. From the temples we all grow
old, and onward to the chin creeps
time, whitening it; one must do something while the knee is green.
15. The Syracusan Women, or the Women at the Adonis Festival
Gorgo
Is Praxinoa at home?
Praxinoa
Dear Gorgo, how long it has been. Yes, at home.
A wonder you have come even now. Get her a chair, Eunoa.
Throw a cushion on it too.
Gorgo
It does very well.
Praxinoa
Sit down.
Gorgo
Oh, what a restless creature I am. I have barely got to you alive,
Praxinoa, through such a crowd, such a press of chariots.
Everywhere boots, everywhere men in cloaks;
and the road endless; and you live ever so far away.
Praxinoa
It is that madman of mine; he came and took a hovel
at the world's end, no house at all, so that we should not be neighbors,
out of pure spite, the jealous wretch, always the same.
Gorgo
Do not speak so of your husband, dear, of Dinon, such things,
with the little one by; look, woman, how he stares at you.
Never mind, Zopyrion, sweet child; she is not talking of daddy.
Praxinoa
The baby understands, by our Lady.
Gorgo
Nice daddy.
Praxinoa
That daddy of ours, the other day—and we say the other day
for everything, of course—went to buy soda and rouge from the stall,
and came back with salt, the great thirteen-foot lout.
Gorgo
Mine is just the same, a waster of money, Diocleidas;
yesterday he gave seven drachmas for what were mere dog-hairs,
pluckings of old wallets, five fleeces, all filth, work on work.
But come, get your wrap and your pinned mantle.
Let us go to rich king Ptolemy's palace
to see the Adonis; I hear the queen
is arranging something fine.
Praxinoa
In a rich house all is rich.
Gorgo
What you have seen, you can tell to one who has not seen it.
It must be time to be going.
Praxinoa
For the idle every day is a holiday.
Eunoa, pick up the wool and lay it down again
in the middle, you lazy thing. The cats want to sleep soft.
Get a move on, bring water quickly. Water is wanted first;
and she brings the soap. Give it anyway. Not so much, you greedy girl.
Pour the water. Wretch, why are you wetting my dress?
Stop. I am washed, such as the gods pleased.
Where is the key of the big chest? Bring it here.
Gorgo
Praxinoa, that gathered robe with its pins
suits you wonderfully; tell me, what did it cost you off the loom?
Praxinoa
Do not remind me, Gorgo; more than a mina of pure silver,
or two; and on the work I put my very soul.
Gorgo
Well, it turned out just as you wished.
Praxinoa
That you may well say.
Bring me my wrap, and set the hat on properly
over my head. I will not take you, child. Bogey-man; the horse bites.
Cry as much as you like, but you must not be made a cripple.
Let us go. Phrygia, take the little one and play with him,
call the dog in, and lock the courtyard door.—
O gods, what a crowd. How and ever shall we get through
this misery? Ants without number or measure.
Many fine deeds, Ptolemy, have you done,
since your father went among the immortals; no malefactor
harms the passer-by, slipping up on him Egyptian fashion,
as before, when men shaped by deceit used to play their tricks,
all alike, vile games, all of one rotten stamp.
Sweetest Gorgo, what will become of us? The king's
war-horses. Dear man, do not trample me.
The chestnut has reared up; see how wild he is. Bold as a dog,
Eunoa, will you not flee? He will be the death of the man who leads him.

title: Idylls
text:
How glad I am that I left my baby at home.
Gorgo
Take heart, Praxinoa; we have got behind them now,
and they have gone to their place.
Praxinoa
And I am collecting myself again now.
A horse and the cold snake are what I have dreaded most
since I was a child. Let us hurry; a great crowd pours toward us.
Gorgo
Are you from the palace, mother?
Old Woman
I am, my children.
Gorgo
Is it easy
to get in?
Old Woman
By trying the Achaeans got into Troy,
fairest of girls; by trying everything is accomplished.
Gorgo
The old woman has delivered her oracle and gone.
Praxinoa
Women know everything, even how Zeus married Hera.
Gorgo
Look, Praxinoa, what a throng about the doors.
Praxinoa
Prodigious. Gorgo, give me your hand; and you too take hold,
Eunoa, of Eutychis; mind you do not get lost.
Let us all go in together; Eunoa, hold tight to us.
Oh dear, my summer-cloak is torn
clean in two already, Gorgo. For Zeus' sake, if you would be
a happy man, sir, mind my wrap.
Stranger
It is not in my power, but I will mind it all the same.
Praxinoa
The crowd is packed close.
They shove like pigs.
Stranger
Take heart, woman; we are well placed.
Praxinoa
And for years to come may you be well placed, dear man,
for sheltering us. A kind and pitiful man.
Eunoa is being crushed by us; come, you faintheart, push.
Splendid. All inside, as the man said who shut his bride in.
Gorgo
Praxinoa, come here. Look first at the embroideries,
how fine and graceful; you would call them robes for the gods.
Praxinoa
Lady Athena, what workwomen wrought them,
what artists drew those exact designs.
How truly they stand, and how truly they move about,
living, not woven. A clever thing is man.
And he himself, how marvelous, lies on the silver
couch, the first down just dropping from his temples,
the thrice-loved Adonis, loved even in Acheron.
Second Stranger
Stop, you wretched women, chattering without end,
you turtle-doves. They will wear one out with their broad drawling.
Gorgo
Goodness, where is the man from? And what is it to you if we are chatterers?
Buy your own slaves and order them about. You give orders to Syracusans?
And, that you may know this too: we are Corinthians by descent,
like Bellerophon; we speak the Peloponnesian way.
I suppose Dorians may speak Doric.
Praxinoa
May Persephone never have a master over us,
save one. I do not care a rap. Do not scrape an empty measure at me.
Gorgo
Hush, Praxinoa; the daughter of the Argive woman is about to sing
the Adonis, that skilled singer,
who last year too won the prize for the dirge.
She will give us something fine, I am sure; she is clearing her throat already.
Woman Singer
Mistress, who loved Golgi and Idalium
and steep Eryx, Aphrodite at play with gold;
see how the soft-footed Hours have brought you Adonis
from ever-flowing Acheron in the twelfth month.
The Hours, slowest of the blessed, dear Hours, yet longed for
they come to all mortals, ever bringing some gift.
Cyprian, daughter of Dione, you, as men's story goes,
made Berenice immortal from a mortal woman,
dropping ambrosia into the woman's breast;
and in thanks to you, goddess of many names and many shrines,
Berenice's daughter, Arsinoe, like Helen,
cherishes Adonis with all fair things.
Beside him lie all the fruits in season that the trees bear at their tops,
and beside him soft gardens kept in little baskets
of silver, and golden flasks of Syrian myrrh.
And all the cakes that women make on the kneading-board,
mingling every kind of flower with white meal,
all that they make of sweet honey or in liquid oil,

title: Idylls
text:
all winged and creeping things are here beside him.
Green bowers are built, weighed down with soft dill;
and the boy Loves flit above,
like young nightingales on the growing trees
that flutter, trying their wings, from branch to branch.
Oh, the ebony, oh, the gold, oh, the eagles of white
ivory that bear to Zeus, son of Cronos, the boy his cupbearer.
And purple coverlets above, softer than sleep;
Miletus will say it, and the man who pastures flocks in Samos;
other couches are spread for the fair Adonis.
One Cypris holds, the other the rosy-armed Adonis,
a bridegroom of eighteen or nineteen years.
His kiss does not prick, for the down is still red about his lips.
Now let Cypris rejoice, having her own husband;
but at dawn, with the dew, we will carry him out together
down to the waves that plash upon the shore,
and loosing our hair and letting our robes fall to our ankles,
with breasts bare, we will begin the clear-voiced song:
You come, dear Adonis, here and to Acheron,
alone, men say, of the demigods. Neither Agamemnon
had this lot, nor great Ajax, the hero of heavy wrath,
nor Hector, eldest of Hecuba's twenty sons,
nor Patroclus, nor Pyrrhus returning from Troy,
nor those still earlier, the Lapiths and the sons of Deucalion,
nor the Pelopids, nor the Argive chiefs, the flower of the Pelasgians.
Be gracious now, dear Adonis, and bless us in the coming year.
Welcome you have come, Adonis, and when you come again, you will come as a friend.
Gorgo
Praxinoa, the woman is a clever creature.
Lucky she, to know so much; thrice lucky, how sweetly she sings.
But it is time, all the same, to go home. Diocleidas has had no dinner.
And the man is all vinegar; when he is hungry, do not even go near him.
Farewell, beloved Adonis; and may you come to us in joy.

title: Idylls
text:
16. The Graces, or Hiero
This is ever the care of the daughters of Zeus, and ever of singers:
to hymn the immortals, to hymn the glorious deeds of good men.
The Muses are goddesses, and goddesses sing of gods;
but we are mortals here, and let mortals sing of mortals.
For who of all who dwell beneath the gray dawn
will open his door and gladly receive my Graces
when they spread their wings, and not send them off again unrewarded?
But they come back home in anger, on bare feet,
reviling me much because they went a fruitless journey,
and reluctant once more, in the bottom of an empty chest,
they remain, their heads cast down upon their cold knees,
where their seat is always, when they return unsuccessful.
Who of men now is of such a kind? Who will love the one who speaks well of him?
I do not know; for men no longer, as before, are eager
to be praised for noble deeds, but are mastered by gain.
Each, with his hands under his cloak, looks about for where he may get
silver, and would not rub the rust off a coin to give to anyone,
but at once declares: The shin is nearer than the knee;
let me have something for myself; the gods honor singers.
And who would listen to another? Homer is enough for all.
He is the best of singers, who shall take nothing from me.
Foolish men, what gain is the countless gold
lying within? This is not what the wise count the use of wealth,
but to give some to one's own soul, and some to a singer,
and to do good service to many kinsmen, and to many other
men besides, and ever to offer altar-sacrifice to the gods,
and not to be a bad host, but having welcomed a guest at table
to send him off when he wishes to depart,
and above all to honor the holy interpreters of the Muses,
so that even when hidden in Hades you may be heard of as noble,
and not lament without glory by cold Acheron,

title: Idylls
text:
like some man with hands callused inside by the mattock,
bewailing the bare poverty he has inherited from his fathers.
Many in the halls of Antiochus and of lord Aleuas
received their monthly measure of food, the bondsmen;
and many calves, driven to the pens of the Scopadae,
lowed along with the horned cattle,
and over the Crannonian plain countless
choice sheep the shepherds folded for the hospitable Creondae;
but no joy of these was theirs, when they had poured out their sweet
life into the wide raft of hateful Acheron,
and, forgotten, leaving behind all those many blessings,
among the wretched dead they lay through long ages,
had not that singer of Ceos, with his varied voice,
set them, named, on the many-stringed lyre among men
