of later days; and even the swift horses won honor,
that came back garlanded for them from the holy games.
And who would ever have known the chiefs of the Lycians, who the long-haired
sons of Priam, or Cycnus pale as a woman in his skin,
had not singers hymned the battles of men of old?
Nor would Odysseus, who wandered a hundred and twenty months
among all peoples, and went living to the farthest Hades,
and escaped the cave of the deadly Cyclops,
have had long-lasting fame; and silent would Eumaeus
the swineherd have been, and Philoetius, busy
with the herded cattle, and great-hearted Laertes himself,
had not the songs of the Ionian man profited them.
From the Muses good fame comes to men,
but the living waste the wealth of the dead.
Yet equal is the labor of measuring the waves upon the shore,
as many as the wind drives landward from the gray sea,
or of washing clean a brick of mud with clear water,
and of trying to win over a man corrupted by love of gain.
Farewell to such a man; let him have countless
silver, and let longing for more ever possess him.

title: Idylls
text:
But I would choose honor and the friendship of men
before many mules and horses.
I seek to whom of mortals I may come welcome
with the Muses; for hard are the roads for singers
without the daughters of Zeus, who counsels greatly.
Not yet has the sky grown weary of leading round the months and the years;
many horses shall yet turn the chariot-wheel;
there shall be a man who will have need of me as his singer,
having done as great deeds as great Achilles or heavy Ajax
in the plain of Simois, where lies the tomb of Phrygian Ilus.
Already now the Phoenicians who dwell beneath the setting sun
on the farthest verge of Libya are shuddering with dread.
Already the Syracusans grip their spears by the middle,
their arms weighed down with shields of willow;
and among them Hiero, equal to the heroes of old,
girds himself, and horsehair plumes shade his helmet.
Would, O most glorious Zeus, father, and lady Athena,
and the Maiden, who with your mother have for your portion the great city
of the rich Ephyraeans by the waters of Lysimeleia,
that an evil necessity might send our enemies out of the island
over the Sardinian wave, bearing word of the death of dear ones
to children and to wives, few to be counted out of many;
and that the cities might again be dwelt in by their former citizens,
all that the enemies' hands ravaged to the ground;
and that men might work the flourishing fields; and that the countless
thousands of sheep, fattened on the pasture,
might bleat over the plain, and that the cattle, coming in herds
to the steading, might hasten the homing wayfarer at dusk;
and that the fallow lands might be worked toward the sowing, when the cicada,
watching the shepherds at noon, sheltered within the trees,
sings in the boughs; and that the spiders might spread their fine
webs over the armor, and that of the war-cry there might not be even a name.

title: Idylls
text:
And may singers carry the high fame of Hiero
both beyond the Scythian sea and to where the broad wall
that Semiramis bound with bitumen reigned over the land.
I am but one, and the daughters of Zeus love many
others too; and may they all care to hymn Sicilian Arethusa
with her peoples, and the spearman Hiero.
O goddesses, daughters of Eteocles, you who love
Minyan Orchomenus, once hateful to Thebes,
unbidden indeed would I stay at home, but to those who call
I would come boldly, with my Muses.
Nor will I leave you behind; for what is dear to men
apart from the Graces? May I be ever with the Graces.

title: Idylls
text:
17. Encomium of Ptolemy
From Zeus let us begin, and with Zeus, Muses, let us end,
whenever in our songs we praise the best of the immortals;
but among men let Ptolemy be named among the first,
and last and midmost; for he is the most eminent of all.
The heroes, who of old sprang from the demigods,
doing fair deeds, found skilled singers;
and I, knowing how to speak fair words, would hymn
Ptolemy; and hymns are the gift of the immortals themselves.
When a woodcutter comes to leafy Ida,
he looks about, with plenty at hand, where to begin his work.
What shall I tell first? For there are countless things to say,
wherein the gods have honored the best of kings.
From his fathers, how able was Ptolemy, son of Lagus,
to accomplish a great deed, when he laid up in his mind
a counsel such as no other man could conceive.
Him the Father set equal in honor with the blessed
immortals, and a golden house is built for him
in the dwelling of Zeus; and beside him sits Alexander,
his loving friend, the god heavy upon the Persians, with his glittering diadem.
And opposite is set the seat of Heracles, slayer of centaurs,
fashioned out of solid adamant;
there with the other sons of heaven he holds his feasts,
rejoicing exceedingly in his grandsons' grandsons,
because the son of Cronos took old age from their limbs,
and his descendants, born of his line, are called immortal.
For to both of them the mighty son of Heracles is forefather,
and both are reckoned back to Heracles at the last.
And so, when he goes from the feast, already sated
with fragrant nectar, to the house of his dear wife,
to the one he gives his bow and the quiver under his arm,
to the other his knotted iron club;
and they bear the weapons and the bearded son of Zeus himself
into the ambrosial chamber of white-ankled Hebe.
And how, among the wise women, renowned Berenice
was preeminent, a great blessing to her parents.
For her the lady daughter of Dione, who holds Cyprus,
pressed her slender hands into her fragrant bosom.
Therefore, they say, no woman ever pleased a man so much
as Ptolemy loved his own wife.
Truly he was loved far more in return; so that with confidence
he might entrust his whole house to his children,
whenever, loving, he goes to the bed of her who loves.
But an unloving woman's heart is always on another,
and her children come easily, but resemble not their father.
You who excel the goddesses in beauty, lady Aphrodite,
she was your care; and for your sake fair Berenice
did not cross woeful Acheron,
but, snatching her away before she came down to the dark ship
and the ever-hateful ferryman of the dead,
you set her in your temple, and gave her a share of your own honors.
Gracious to all mortals, she breathes soft loves
upon them, and gives light cares to the one who longs.—
Dark-browed Argive woman, you bore Diomedes, slayer of men,
mingling with Tydeus, the Calydonian man;
but deep-bosomed Thetis bore the spearman Achilles
to Peleus, son of Aeacus; and you, spearman Ptolemy,
illustrious Berenice bore to the spearman Ptolemy.
And Cos reared you, a newborn babe,
receiving you from your mother, when you first saw the dawn.
For there the daughter of Antigone, weighed down with the pangs of birth,
called upon Eileithyia who loosens the girdle;
and she stood graciously beside her, and shed
a painlessness over all her limbs; and a child like his father,
a beloved child, was born. And Cos cried out with joy at the sight,
and said, touching the babe with loving hands:
Be blessed, boy, and may you honor me as much

title: Idylls
text:
as Phoebus Apollo honored dark-crowned Delos;
and set the Triopian hill in equal honor,
granting the Dorians who are near an equal portion of esteem;
equally too did lord Apollo love Rheneia.
So the island spoke; and from on high, three times,
a great eagle, the bird of omen, cried out from the clouds.
This was a sign from Zeus, I think. To Zeus, son of Cronos, belong
the reverend kings; and he is preeminent whom Zeus loves
from his very birth; and much prosperity attends him,
and he rules over much land and much sea.
Countless continents and countless nations of men
make the grain grow, increased by the rain of Zeus;
but none brings forth so much as low-lying Egypt,
when the Nile, gushing up, breaks the moist clods.
Nor does any hold so many cities of men skilled in works.
Three hundreds of cities are built in his land,
and three thousands besides three myriads,
and twice three, and after them three nines;
and over all of them Ptolemy the valiant reigns.
And he cuts off for himself part of Phoenicia and of Arabia
and of Syria and Libya and the dark Ethiopians.
He gives the word to all the Pamphylians and the spearmen Cilicians,
to the Lycians and the war-loving Carians,
and to the Cyclades islands, since his ships are the best
that sail the sea; and all the sea and land
and the sounding rivers are ruled by Ptolemy.
Many horsemen, many shield-bearing men,
decked in gleaming bronze, gather about him.
In wealth he might outweigh all kings;
so much comes each day to his rich house
from every side. And his peoples ply their work in peace.
For no enemy crossing the Nile teeming with sea-beasts
has on foot raised a war-cry among foreign villages,
nor has any leapt to the shore from a swift ship,
armed and hostile, against the Egyptian cattle;
such a man is established in the broad plains,
golden-haired Ptolemy, skilled to brandish the spear,
whose chief care is to guard all his father's realm,
as a good king should, and what he adds himself.
Nor does gold lie idle and useless in his rich house,
heaped up like the wealth of ever-toiling ants;
but the glorious houses of the gods have much of it,
as he ever offers first-fruits with other honors,
and much he has given to mighty kings,
much to cities, much to his good companions.
Nor has any man come skilled to raise the clear song
at the holy contests of Dionysus,
to whom he did not give a gift worthy of his art.
And the interpreters of the Muses sing of Ptolemy
in return for his good deeds. And what could be finer for a man
of wealth than to win fair fame among men?
This abides even for the sons of Atreus; but all those countless things,
all that they won when they took the great house of Priam,
are hidden somewhere in the air, whence there is no more return.
But he alone of men of old, and of those whose still warm
footprints are pressed and imprinted beneath their feet,
has raised fragrant temples to his dear mother and father;
and in them, beautiful with gold and ivory,
he has set them as helpers to all who dwell on earth.
And many fattened thighs of cattle he burns
as the months come round, upon the reddened altars,
he himself and his mighty wife, than whom no better
woman in the halls embraces a bridegroom in her arms,
loving from her heart both brother and husband.
So too was accomplished the holy marriage of the immortals,
whom queenly Rhea bore as kings of Olympus;
and one bed Iris, still a maiden, having purified her hands
with perfumes, spreads for Zeus and Hera to lie upon.
Farewell, lord Ptolemy; and of you, as of the other

title: Idylls
text:
demigods, I will make mention; and I think I shall utter a word
not to be cast aside by men to come; but for virtue, ask it of Zeus.
18. The Epithalamium of Helen
Once, then, in Sparta, at the house of golden-haired Menelaus,
maidens with blooming hyacinth in their hair
set up a dance before the newly painted bridal chamber,
the first twelve of the city, a great glory of Laconian women,
when the younger son of Atreus, having wooed
the beloved Helen, shut her in with him.
And all of them sang, beating time to one strain
with their interweaving feet, and the house rang with the wedding-song.
So early then have you fallen asleep, dear bridegroom?
Are you too heavy in the knee? Are you fond of sleep?
Did you drink deep, when you flung yourself into bed?
If you were so eager to sleep at the proper hour, you should have slept alone,
and left the girl to play with girls beside her loving mother
till deep dawn, since both tomorrow and on the morrow,
and from year to year, Menelaus, this is your bride.
Happy bridegroom, some good man sneezed for you as you came
to Sparta, like the other chiefs, that you might succeed.
Alone among the demigods you shall have Zeus, son of Cronos, for father-in-law.
The daughter of Zeus has come beneath one blanket with you,
such as no other of the Achaean women treads the earth.
Surely she will bear some great child, if she bears one like the mother.
We all, her companions of one age, who ran the same course,
anointed like men, by the baths of the Eurotas,
four times sixty girls, the maiden youth of the land,
of whom not one is without fault, when she is matched with Helen.
The rising Dawn shows a fair face,
lady Night, and the white spring when winter is loosed;
so too golden Helen shone among us.
As the tall grain rises, an ornament to the rich field,
or the cypress to the garden, or the Thessalian horse to the chariot,
so rosy-skinned Helen is an ornament to Lacedaemon.
No one winds from the basket such work as hers,
nor in the carven loom, weaving with the shuttle,
cut from the long beams a closer web.
Nor does anyone know how to strike the lyre so,
singing of Artemis and broad-breasted Athena,
as Helen, in whose eyes all desires dwell.
O fair, O graceful girl, you are now a housewife;
but we will go at dawn to the running-ground and to the meadow grasses
to gather sweet-breathing garlands,
remembering you much, Helen, as suckling
lambs long for the teat of the ewe that bore them.
First of all we will plait you a garland of low-growing lotus
and lay it under a shady plane-tree,
and first, taking liquid oil from a silver flask,
we will let it drip beneath the shady plane-tree;
and letters will be written on the bark, that a passer-by
may read, in Dorian fashion: Worship me; I am Helen's tree.
Farewell, bride; farewell, bridegroom with the noble father-in-law.
May Leto grant you, Leto the nurse of children,
a fair offspring; and may Cypris, the goddess Cypris, grant equal love
for each other; and may Zeus, Zeus son of Cronos, grant imperishable wealth,
that it may pass from noble to noble again.
Sleep, breathing love and longing into each other's breast,
but do not forget to wake at dawn.
We too will return at morning, when the first singer
lifts his fair-feathered neck from his perch and crows.
Hymen, O Hymenaeus, rejoice in this marriage.
19. The Honey-Thief
Love the thief was once stung cruelly by a bee
as he was robbing a honeycomb from the hives, and it pricked
all his fingertips. And he was in pain, and blew on his hand,

title: Idylls
text:
and stamped the ground and leapt, and to Aphrodite
he showed his hurt and complained that so small
a creature is the bee, and what great wounds it makes.
And his mother laughed: What of it? Are you not the bee's equal?
For you are small, yet what great wounds you make.
20. The Young Cowherd
Eunica laughed at me when I wished to kiss her sweetly,
and mocking me she said these words: Get away from me.
A cowherd, and you want to kiss me, wretch? I have not learned
to kiss country fashion, but to press town-bred lips.
Do not kiss my fair mouth, not even in your dreams.
How you stare, what stuff you talk, how boorishly you play,
how daintily you wheedle, what coaxing words you say;
how soft a beard you have, how sweet a head of hair.
Your lips are diseased, and your hands are black,
and you smell foul. Away from me, lest you defile me.
So speaking she spat three times into her bosom,
and eyed me steadily from head to foot,
curling her lips and looking sidelong with her eyes,
and gave herself great airs of beauty, and grinning
scornfully she laughed at me. And straightway my blood boiled,
and my skin flushed red with pain, like a rose with the dew.
And she went off and left me; and I carry anger beneath my heart,
that the vile wench mocked me, the graceful one.
Shepherds, tell me the truth: am I not handsome?
Has some god of a sudden made me into another man?
For before this a sweet beauty bloomed on me
like ivy on a tree-trunk, and shaded my chin,
and my locks fell about my temples like wild celery,
and my white forehead shone above black brows;
my eyes were far brighter than gray-eyed Athena's,
and my mouth sweeter than curd, and from my mouth
flowed a voice sweeter than honey from the comb.
And sweet is my music, whether I make melody on the pipe,
or sound the flute, or the reed, or the cross-flute.
And all the women on the hills call me handsome,
and all of them kiss me; but the town girl did not kiss me,
but, because I am a cowherd, ran past and never listens,
though the fair Dionysus drove a heifer in the glens.
She did not know that Cypris went mad for a herdsman
and pastured cattle in the Phrygian hills, and loved Adonis
in the woodlands, and in the woodlands wept for him.
And who was Endymion? Was he not a cowherd? Whom the Moon
loved as he herded, and coming from Olympus
came secretly to the glade and slept beside the boy.
And you, Rhea, weep for your cowherd. And did not you too,
son of Cronos, for the sake of a herd-boy, wander as a bird?
But Eunica alone would not kiss the cowherd,
she who is greater than Cybele and Cypris and the Moon.
No more, then, Cypris, may you kiss your sweet one, either in the town
or on the hill, but sleep alone through the night.
21. The Fishermen
Poverty alone, Diophantus, rouses the arts,
she herself the teacher of toil; for evil cares
do not even let working men sleep.
And if one closes his eyes for a little of the night, the cares
that stand over him suddenly trouble his sleep.
Two old fishermen lay together,
having spread dry seaweed under their wickerwork hut,
leaning against the wall of leaves; and near them
lay the implements of their hands, the baskets,
the rods, the hooks, the weed-grown baits,
lines, weels, and labyrinths of rushes,
cords, an oar, and an old boat on its props;
beneath their heads a thin mat, and clothes upon them.
This was all the fishermen's livelihood, this their wealth.
Neither had so much as a coverlet or nets; all was superfluous,
all seemed so to them; for poverty wore them down.

title: Idylls
text:
No neighbor lived between them; and beside their hut,
pressed close by poverty, the sea murmured softly.
Not yet had the chariot of the Moon finished its midmost course,
when their familiar toil woke the fishermen, and from their eyelids
thrusting off sleep, they stirred speech in their minds.
Asphalion
They all lie, my friend, who said the nights
grow shorter in summer, when Zeus brings the long days.
Already I have seen ten thousand dreams, and it is not yet dawn.
Am I mistaken? What is the matter? The nights are endless.
Companion
Asphalion, do you blame the fair summer? For the season
has not of itself passed beyond its course; but care
cutting your sleep makes the night seem long to you.
Asphalion
Have you ever learned to interpret dreams? For I saw a good one.
I do not want you to have no share of my vision.
Just as with the catch, share out all the dreams between us.
For he who guesses by his wits is the best
interpreter of dreams; the teacher is the one who has sense.
Besides, we have leisure; for what could a man do
lying among leaves by the water, and not sleeping,
but like the ass among the brambles or the lamp in the town-hall;
for they say it never sleeps.
Companion
Then tell me your vision of the night,
since a man tells what he knows to his comrade.
Asphalion
As I fell asleep at evening, after my labors on the sea
(I had not eaten much, for dining early,
if you remember, we spared our bellies), I saw myself
busy upon a rock, and sitting I watched
for fish, and from my rod I shook the deceiving bait.
And one of the fat ones snapped at it; for in their sleep
every dog dreams of bread, and I of fish.
And it clung to the hook, and the blood flowed,
and with its struggling I held the rod bent,
my hands strained and curved, a hard contest,
how to land so great a fish with my weak iron.
Then, reminding it of its wound, I gently pricked it,
and having pricked I gave it line, and since it did not flee I drew it in.
So I finished the contest, and hauled up a golden fish,
all overlaid with gold; and I was afraid
it might be a fish dear to Poseidon,
or perhaps a treasure of gray-eyed Amphitrite.
And gently I loosed it from the hook,
lest the barbs should keep any gold from its mouth.
And I trusted, calling out, that it was the lovely fish,
and I swore that I would never again set foot upon the sea,
but would stay on land and be a king with my gold.
This is what woke me; and you, stranger, now lend
your judgment; for I am afraid of the oath I swore.
Companion
And you, why do you fear? You swore no oath; for you did not even find
the golden fish you saw, but the vision was no better than lies,
the empty hope of dreams. Seek the fish of flesh,
if perhaps, still drowsing, you go on hunting these vain things,
lest you die of hunger, for all your golden dreams.
22. The Dioscuri
We sing of the two sons of Leda and of Zeus, lord of the aegis,
Castor, and Polydeuces, dread to provoke in boxing
when he has bound his hands amid the thongs of oxhide.
Twice and a third time we sing the male children
of the Thestiad maiden, the two Lacedaemonian brothers,
saviors of men when they are already on the razor's edge,
and of horses thrown into confusion in the bloody throng,
and of ships that, defying the setting and the rising
stars of heaven, have met with cruel gales.
The winds raise a great wave against their stern,
or from the prow, or wherever each wind's will is,
and fling it into the hold, and shatter both
the sides; and all the tackle hangs with the sail,

title: Idylls
text:
snapped off at random; and much rain pours from heaven
as night comes on; and the wide sea roars,
beaten by the blasts and the unbreaking hail.
But even so you draw the ships up from the deep,
with the very sailors who thought they would die;
and at once the winds cease, and a shining calm
is over the sea; and the clouds run apart this way and that;
and the Bears appear, and between the Asses the dim
Manger, betokening all fair weather for sailing.
O helpers of mortals, both of you, both dear,
horsemen, lyre-players, athletes, singers;
shall I begin to sing first of Castor, or of Polydeuces?
Hymning both, I will sing first of Polydeuces.
Now Argo, having escaped the rocks that clash into one
and the deadly mouth of snowy Pontus,
came to the Bebrycians, bearing the dear children of the gods.
There down a single ladder from both
sides of Jason's ship many men descended.
Going ashore upon the deep sand and the sheltered beach
they spread their beds and worked the fire-sticks in their hands.
But Castor of the swift colts and ruddy Polydeuces
both wandered alone, straying from their comrades,
gazing on the wild woodland of every kind upon the mountain.
They found an ever-flowing spring under a smooth rock,
filled with water unpolluted; and below
the pebbles showed like crystal and silver
from the depth; and tall pines grew near,
and white poplars and plane-trees and tufted cypresses,
and fragrant flowers, dear works to the shaggy bees,
all that teem over the meadows at the ending of spring.
There a monstrous man sat in the open,
dread to behold, his ears crushed with hard fists;
his huge chest was rounded, and his back broad,
with iron flesh, like a hammered colossus.
And on his solid arms, below the top of the shoulder,
the muscles stood like rounded boulders, which a torrent
river, rolling them, has polished round in its great eddies;
and over his back and neck there hung,
slung by the paws, a lion's skin.
To him first the prize-winning Polydeuces spoke.
Polydeuces
Hail, stranger, whoever you are. What men are these, whose land is this?
Amycus
How am I to be glad, when I see men I have not seen before?
Polydeuces
Take heart. Do not think you look on unjust men or on the sons of unjust men.
Amycus
I take heart, and it is not from you that I need to learn that.
Polydeuces
Are you savage, ill-tempered toward all, or insolent?
Amycus
Such as you see; and at least I do not trespass on your land.
Polydeuces
Come, then, and having had a guest's gifts you may go home again.
Amycus
Do not entertain me, and what is from me is not ready either.
Polydeuces
Strange man, would you not even give me a drink of this water?
Amycus
You will know it, if thirst parches your dry lips.
Polydeuces
Silver, or what is the price, tell me, by which we might persuade you?
Amycus
Raise your hands, one against one, standing face to face with your man.
Polydeuces
A boxer, or one who strikes the leg too with the foot?
Amycus
. . . With your eyes straight ahead,
strain at the boxing, and do not spare your skill.
Polydeuces
And who is he against whom I am to set my hands and my thongs?
Amycus
You see him near; the boxer will not be called a woman.
Polydeuces
And is there a prize ready, for which we two shall contend?
Amycus
I shall be yours, and you shall be called mine, if I win.
Polydeuces
Such are the battles of crested cocks.
Amycus
Then, whether we are like cocks or lions,
we will not fight for any other prize.
So spoke Amycus, and taking a hollow shell he blew a blast.

title: Idylls
text:
And quickly the long-haired Bebrycians gathered
beneath the shady plane-trees at the blowing of the shell.
So too Castor, preeminent in war, went and called
all the heroes from the Magnesian ship.
And when they had strengthened their hands with thongs
of oxhide and wound the long straps about their arms,
they came together into the midst, breathing slaughter at each other.
There much labor befell them in their eagerness,
which of them should get the light of the sun behind his back;
by your skill you slipped past the great man, Polydeuces,
and all the face of Amycus was struck by the rays.
But he, angered in his heart, rushed forward,
aiming with his hands. As he came on, the son of Tyndareus
struck the tip of his chin; and he was stirred more than before,
and joined battle in confusion, and bore down heavily, leaning
toward the ground. The Bebrycians cheered, and on the other side
the heroes encouraged mighty Polydeuces,
fearing lest somehow, bearing down on him, he might overpower him
in the narrow space, a man like Tityus.
But the son of Zeus, taking his stand here and there,
cut him with both hands by turns, and checked the rush
of the son of Poseidon, overweening as he was.
He stood reeling with the blows, and spat out crimson
blood; and all the chiefs together shouted,
as they saw the grievous wounds about his mouth and jaws;
and his eyes were narrowed in his swollen face.
Then the lord confounded him, feinting idly with his hands
on every side; but when he saw him at a loss,
he drove his fist above the middle of his nose, beneath the brow,
and tore all his forehead to the bone. And he, struck,
was stretched on his back among the flourishing leaves.
There a bitter fight arose again when he stood up;
and they slew each other, smiting with the hard thongs.
But he, the chief of the Bebrycians, plied his hands
at the chest and outside the neck; while with unsightly blows
the unconquered Polydeuces mangled all his face.
And his flesh shrank with sweat, and from a great man
he soon became small; while the other ever bore limbs
grown sturdier as the toil went on, and better in color.
How then did the son of Zeus bring down the gluttonous man?
Tell, goddess, for you know; and I, the interpreter of others,
will speak as you will, and however it is dear to you yourself.
Now he, longing to do some great deed,
seized with his left the left hand of Polydeuces,
leaning aside from his guard, and stepping in with the other
he brought up his broad fist from his right flank.
And had it reached him, he would have hurt the king of Amyclae;
but he ducked his head aside, and with his strong hand at the same time
struck him under the left temple and threw his weight on the shoulder;
and the black blood gushed swiftly from the gaping temple;
and with his left he smote the mouth, and the close-set teeth rattled;
and ever with a sharper rain of blows he marred the face,
until he crushed the cheeks. And on the ground he lay
senseless, and held up both his hands together,
renouncing the fight, since he was near to death.
And though you had the mastery, you did him no wanton wrong,
boxer Polydeuces; but he swore you a great oath,
calling on his father Poseidon out of the sea,
never again of his own will to be grievous to strangers.
And so you are hymned by me, lord. And you, Castor, I will sing,
son of Tyndareus, swift with the colts, spear-wielder, bronze-armored.
The two sons of Zeus had snatched up and were carrying off
the two daughters of Leucippus; and the two of them in turn,

title: Idylls
text:
the brother sons of Aphareus, were pursuing them hotly,
the bridegrooms-to-be, Lynceus and mighty Idas.
But when they came to the tomb of dead Aphareus,
all together they leapt from their chariots upon each other,
weighed down with spears and hollow shields.
And Lynceus spoke out, shouting loud from beneath his helmet:
Strange men, why are you so eager for battle? How are you so harsh
over other men's brides, with bare swords in your hands?
To us Leucippus betrothed these his daughters,
to us long before; this marriage was sworn to us;
but you, against all decency, with other men's beds in view,
with cattle and mules and other goods
have turned the man aside, and stolen the marriage with gifts.
Truly, often before to your faces, to both of you,
I myself said this, though I am no man of many words:
It is not thus, dear men, that it befits chiefs
to woo wives for whom bridegrooms are already ready.
Wide is Sparta, wide is Elis where horses run,
and Arcadia rich in flocks, and the cities of the Achaeans,
and Messene and Argos and all the Sisyphian shore;
there are reared, beneath their own parents,
countless girls, lacking neither in form nor in sense.
Of these it is easy for you to marry whichever you wish;
for many would wish to be the fathers-in-law of good men;
and you are distinguished among all heroes,
both your fathers and, from above, all your fathers' blood.
But, friends, let this marriage come to its end
for us; and for you two let us all devise another.
Many such things I urged, but they went off into the wet wave,
borne by the wind's breath, and no grace followed my words.
For you two are not to be charmed, and are pitiless. But even now
be persuaded; for both of you are our cousins on the father's side.
But if your hearts long for war, and we must
break out the kindred strife and bathe our spears in blood,
then let Idas, and my own brother, mighty Polydeuces,
hold back their hands from the hateful fray,
and let us two, I and Castor, decide it in battle,
being the younger born. And let us not leave too great a grief
for our parents. Enough is one corpse from one house;
and the rest, all of them, will gladden their comrades,
bridegrooms instead of corpses, and will wed these
girls; with a small evil it is fitting to end a great quarrel.
So he spoke; and the god was not to make his words vain.
For the two who were the elder in birth took the armor
from their shoulders to the ground; and Lynceus came into the midst,
shaking his strong spear beneath the rim of his shield;
and so likewise Castor leveled the sharp points
of his spear; and the plumes nodded on both their crests.
First with their spears, aiming, they had labor
with each other, if anywhere they might see a part of the flesh bared.
But the spear-points, before they had hurt either man,
were broken, fixed in the dread shields.
Then both, drawing their swords from the scabbard, again
wrought slaughter on each other; and there was no respite from the fight.
Many a thrust at the broad shield and the horsehair-crested helmet
Castor made, and many a thrust, exact of eye, did Lynceus make
at the other's shield, and his point reached only as far as the crimson crest.
But Castor lopped off the tip of his hand at the wrist
as he carried the sharp sword, stepping up under it with his left
foot; and Lynceus, struck, dropped his sword, and at once turned to flee
toward his father's tomb, where mighty Idas
lay leaning and watched the kindred battle of the men.
But the son of Tyndareus, darting after him, drove the broad sword

title: Idylls
text:
clean through his flank and his navel; and the bronze at once
scattered his entrails within; and Lynceus fell forward on his face,
and heavy sleep ran down upon his eyelids.
Nor indeed did Laocoosa see the other of her sons
at his father's hearth accomplishing a happy marriage.
For Messenian Idas, swiftly tearing up the standing pillar
from the tomb of Aphareus,
was about to hurl it at the slayer of his own brother;
but Zeus came to the rescue, and struck the carved marble
from his hands, and consumed Idas himself with the flaming thunderbolt.
So it is no light thing to war against the sons of Tyndareus.
They themselves prevail, and they are sprung from one who prevailed.
Hail, children of Leda, and to our hymns send
ever a noble glory; for dear are all singers
to the sons of Tyndareus and to Helen and to the other heroes
who laid Ilium waste, helping Menelaus.
For you, lords, the Chian singer wrought renown,
hymning the city of Priam and the ships of the Achaeans
and the battles of Ilium and Achilles, that tower of the war-cry;
and to you I too bring the soothing strains of the clear-voiced Muses,
such as they themselves provide and as my house affords.
And of all gifts to the gods, songs are the fairest.
23. The Lover
A man much given to love loved a cruel youth,
fair in form, but no longer like it in his ways.
He hated the one who loved him and had no gentleness at all,
and did not know what a god Love was, how great a bow
he holds in his hands, how bitter the shafts he drives into the heart;
and in all his words and meetings he was unyielding.
There was no comfort for the flames, no flash
of the lip, no bright gleam of the eyes, no rosy cheek,
no word, no kiss, that might lighten the love.
But as a beast of the wood looks askance at the hunters,
so he did everything toward his lover; savage were his
lips, and his eyes had a dreadful look; for he was full of pride;
and his face changed color with his anger, and the bloom fled from his skin,
clothed about with the insolence of his wrath. Yet even so
he was fair; by his anger the lover was the more inflamed.
At last he could not bear so great a flame of the Cytherean,
but came and wept before the gloomy house,
and kissed the doorpost, and lifted up his voice thus:
Savage and gloomy boy, nursling of an evil lioness,
stony boy and unworthy of love, I have come to bring you
these last gifts, my noose; no longer, boy, do I wish
to vex you, angered as I am with grief, but I go
where you have condemned me, where they say is the common
path for all, where for lovers is the drug of forgetfulness.
But even if I take it all and drain it to my lip,
not even so shall I quench my pain. Now I bid
farewell to your doorway. I know what is to come.
The rose too is fair, and time withers it;
the violet too is fair in spring, and quickly grows old;
white is the lily, and it withers when it falls;
and the snow is white, and it melts when it is spread out.
And a boy's beauty is fair, but lives a little while.
That hour will come when you too shall love,
when you shall weep salt tears, your heart on fire.
But you, boy, do at the last this one sweet thing:
when, coming out, you see the wretched man hung
at your doorway, do not pass me by,
but stand and weep a little, and, pouring out a tear,
loose me from the rope, and put about me from your own limbs
your clothes, and hide me; and once more, at the last, kiss me,
and grant your lips even to the dead. Do not fear me;
I cannot grieve you; you will reconcile me by a kiss.

title: Idylls
text:
And heap me a mound of earth that will hide my love.
And as you go, cry this over me three times: Friend, you lie dead.
And, if you will, this also: My fair comrade is lost.
And write this writing too, which I will scratch upon your walls:
This man Love killed. Wayfarer, do not pass by,
but stand and say this: He had a cruel comrade.
So speaking, he set a stone, and leaning against the wall
up to the middle of the threshold, he fastened from it the dread stone,
the slender cord, and threw the noose about his neck,
and rolled the seat out from under his foot, and hung there
dead. And the youth opened the doors and saw the dead man
hanging from his own courtyard, and was not bent
in his soul, nor wept the fresh slaying, but on the corpse
he defiled all his clothes, and went to the youths' contests
of the wrestling-schools, and sought eagerly his beloved baths,
and came to the god whom he had outraged; and from the stone
base he stepped into the water; and from above
the statue too leapt upon him, and slew the evil youth;
and the stream was reddened; and the boy's voice came up from the water.
Rejoice, you lovers; for the hater was slain.
And love, you haters; for the god knows how to judge.
24. The Little Heracles
When Heracles was ten months old, Alcmena of Midea once
took him and Iphicles, a night younger,
and having bathed them both and filled them with milk,
laid them in a bronze shield, the fair piece of armor
that Amphitryon had stripped from fallen Pterelaus.
And touching the heads of her children the woman said:
Sleep, my babes, a sweet sleep from which you will wake;
sleep, my soul, two brothers, children safe and sound;
blessed may you lie, and blessed may you come to the dawn.
So saying, she rocked the great shield, and sleep took them.
But at the hour when at midnight the Bear turns toward its setting
right over against Orion, who shows his great shoulder,
then crafty Hera sent two dread monsters,
serpents bristling under their dark coils,
upon the broad threshold, where the hollow door-posts
of the doorway stood, threatening to devour the babe Heracles.
And the two, uncoiling along the ground, both rolled
their blood-hungry bellies; and from their eyes an evil fire
flashed as they came, and they spat out a heavy venom.
But when, with darting tongues, they came near the children,
then they woke, by the will of Zeus who notices all things,
the dear children of Alcmena, and light arose throughout the house.
He at once cried out, as soon as he marked the evil beasts
over the hollow shield and saw their shameless fangs,
Iphicles, and kicked off the woolen coverlet with his feet,
eager to flee; but Heracles met them with his hands,
and bound them both in a heavy bond,
gripping their throats, where the baneful poisons are hidden
in deadly serpents, which even the gods abhor.
And the two wound their coils about the late-born,
milk-fed child, who under his nurse's care had never wept;
but again they unwound them when they grew weary of straining,
trying to find release from the forced bond.
And Alcmena heard the cry and was the first to wake:
Rise, Amphitryon; for a chill fear holds me;
rise, and do not put sandals on your feet.
Do you not hear how the younger of the children cries out?
Or do you not see that, though it is the dead of night,
all the walls are clear, as in the pure dawn?
There is something new in the house, dear husband.
So she spoke; and he came down from the bed, obeying his wife,
and reached for his richly wrought sword, which always hung

title: Idylls
text:
above the cedar bedstead on its peg.
He grasped for the newly woven baldric,
lifting in his other hand the great scabbard, a work of lotus-wood.
But the wide chamber was filled again with darkness;
and then he called to the slaves who were breathing heavy sleep:
Bring fire as quickly as you can, taking it from the hearth,
my slaves, and throw back the strong bolts of the doors.
Rise, you stout-hearted slaves. The master is calling.
So spoke the Phoenician woman who had her bed at the mill.
And the slaves came quickly with kindled lamps;
and the house was filled, as each one hastened.
And when they saw the suckling Heracles
holding the two beasts fast in his tender hands,
they cried out together; but he showed the creatures
to his father Amphitryon, and leapt up high, rejoicing
in his boyish triumph, and laughing he laid before his father's feet
the dread monsters now lulled in death.
Then Alcmena gathered to her own bosom
the dry, pale, terrified Iphicles;
and Amphitryon laid the other child beneath the lambswool coverlet,
and going back to bed bethought him of his rest.
The cocks were just singing the third and last dawn-song;
then Alcmena called the seer Teiresias, who always spoke the truth,
and told him the strange portent,
and bade him reveal how it was to be accomplished.
And though the gods purpose something evil,
do not in shame hide it from me; for even so men cannot escape
what Fate hastens from her spindle.
Son of Eueres, I teach you, who know full well.
So much the queen said; and he answered her thus:
Take heart, woman who have borne the noblest, blood of Perseus;
take heart; and lay up in your mind the better part of what is to come.
For by my sweet light, long since gone from my eyes,
many of the Achaean women, rubbing the soft thread
upon their knees with their hands, shall sing at nightfall
of Alcmena by name, and you shall be a reverence to the Argive women.
Such a man is this your son, who shall mount
to the star-bearing heaven, a hero broad of chest,
to whom all wild beasts and all other men shall be inferior.
It is fated that, when he has accomplished twelve labors,
he shall dwell in the house of Zeus, and the Trachinian pyre shall hold all that is mortal of him.
And he shall be called the son-in-law of the immortals, who roused these
lurking beasts to destroy the babe.
That day shall come, when the sharp-toothed wolf,
seeing the fawn in its lair, will not wish to harm it.
But, woman, let the fire be ready beneath the ashes,
and prepare dry sticks of camel-thorn or of buckthorn
or of bramble, or the dry wild pear shaken by the wind;
and burn these two serpents on the wild billets
at midnight, just when they themselves wished to kill your child.
And at dawn let one of the handmaids gather the ash of the fire
and carry it well, all of it, across the river,
and fling it among the jagged rocks beyond the border, and return
without looking back; and first purify the house with pure brimstone,
and then, as is the custom, with pure water mixed with salt
sprinkle it from a garlanded branch, water that does no harm;
and sacrifice a male boar to Zeus the supreme,
that you may ever be supreme over your enemies.
He spoke, and pushing back his ivory chair
Teiresias went off, heavy though he was with his many years.
And Heracles grew up beneath his mother, like a young plant in an orchard,
called the son of Argive Amphitryon.
Letters the old man Linus taught the boy,
son of Apollo, a watchful guardian, a hero,
and to draw the bow and aim true with arrows,

title: Idylls
text:
Eurytus, rich from his fathers in broad acres.
And he made him a singer and shaped both his hands
upon the boxwood lyre, the sweet-singing son of Philammon.
And all the tricks by which the hip-twisting men of Argos
throw each other in wrestling, and all that boxers
skilled with the thongs, and all the holds the all-in fighters
falling to the ground have devised, useful to their art,
he learned, taught by the son of Hermes,
Harpalycus of Phanote, whom not even seeing him from afar
would any man boldly await as he contended in the games;
so dread a frown lay upon his grim face.
And to drive horses under the chariot, and safely round the post
to turn the wheel, guarding the nave,
Amphitryon himself, with loving mind, taught his son,
since he had won very many treasures from the swift games
in horse-pasturing Argos, and the chariots
he mounted kept their straps unbroken till time loosed them.
And to reach at a man with leveled spear, his shoulder under the shield,
and to bear the gash of swords,
and to marshal the ranks, and to measure out an ambush
of the enemy as they came on, and to give commands to horsemen,
Castor, son of Hippalus, taught him, when he came an exile from Argos,
at the time when Tydeus dwelt, having received from Adrastus
all his portion and the great vineyard, in horse-driving Argos.
And among the demigods no other warrior was like Castor
before old age wore away his youth.
So his dear mother had Heracles taught.
And the boy's bed was made near his father's,
a lion's skin most pleasing to him,
and his dinner was roasted meat and a great Dorian loaf
in a basket; surely it would satisfy a man who digs in the vineyard.
But by day he took a small meal without fire.
And he wore plain clothes that reached below his knees.
25. Heracles the Lion-Slayer
And the old man, the ploughman who guarded the plants, addressed him,
ceasing from the work that lay in his hands:
Gladly, stranger, will I tell you all you ask,
revering the dread regard of Hermes of the wayside;
for they say he is angered most of the gods of heaven,
if anyone refuses a traveler in sore need of the road.
The fleecy flocks of king Augeas
do not all graze on one pasture, nor in one place;
but some are on the banks of flowing Elisous,
some by the holy stream of divine Alpheus,
some at Buprasium rich in clusters, and some even here.
And separate folds are built for each of them.
But for the herds, numberless though they all are,
there are pastures here ever flourishing,
a great marsh of the Menius, since dewy meadows
and water-meadows bloom with grass of many kinds
in plenty, which fosters the strength of the horned cattle.
And here on your right hand their steading
shows clear, all of it, beyond the flowing river,
over there, where the spreading plane-trees grow
and the green wild olive, the holy and pure sanctuary
of Apollo the herdsman, stranger, the god most perfect in fulfillment.
And close by, ample quarters are built for the country folk,
who guard for the king his great and unspeakable wealth
with diligence, casting the seed sometimes on fallow ground
thrice-ploughed, and likewise on fourfold-ploughed.
The hard-working vine-diggers know the bounds,
and come to the wine-vats when the ripe summer comes.
For all this plain belongs to wise Augeas,
both the wheat-bearing fields and the tree-clad orchards,
up to the edges of the spring-fed ridge,
which we ply with our labors all day long,
as is right for laborers, whose life is upon the land.
But do you tell me, for it will be the more to your own profit,

title: Idylls
text:
in need of whom you have come here,
whether you are seeking Augeas himself or one of his
slaves who serve him. And I, who know well,
would tell you exactly, since I declare you are not sprung from base men,
nor born yourself resembling base men,
such a great form distinguishes you. Surely the children
of the immortals are such as this among mortals.
And the mighty son of Zeus answered him:
Yes, old man, I would gladly see Augeas, lord of the Epeians;
for it is need of him that has brought me here.
But if he stays in the city among his citizens,
caring for the people, while they judge the suits,
then point me out, old man, leading the way, some servant of his,
whoever is the elder overseer of these fields,
to whom I may say my errand and learn from his telling.
For god has made each man dependent on another.
And the noble ploughman answered him again:
By the counsel of some of the immortals, stranger, you come here,
so that at once all your need is fulfilled.
For thus Augeas, the dear son of Helios,
with his own son, the might of glorious Phyleus,
came yesterday from the city, after many days,
to look over his possessions, which are numberless in the fields;
for so it seems even to kings in their own minds
that the house is safer when they care for it themselves.
But let us go straight to him; and I will lead you
to our steading, where we may find the king.
So saying he led the way, and pondered much in his mind,
seeing the beast's hide and the hand-filling club,
whence the stranger was; and he kept longing to ask him;
but again in hesitation he checked the word as it came to his lip,
lest he should say something out of season
to the man in his haste; for it is hard to know another's mind.
And the dogs, as they drew near, soon perceived them from afar,
both by the scent of the body and the noise of their feet.
And barking wondrously they ran from this side and that
at Heracles, the son of Amphitryon; but about the old man
they fawned on the other side, with idle yelping.
He with stones lifted only just from the ground
scared them to flee back again, and harshly with his voice
he threatened them all, and stopped them from their barking,
glad in his heart that they guarded the steading
even when he was not there; and he spoke such a word:
Ah me, what a creature this is that the lord gods
have made to dwell among men, so thoughtful.
If only it had wits as understanding within,
and knew with whom it ought to be angry and with whom not,
then none of the beasts would dispute with it for honor;
but as it is, it is too quick to wrath and savage for nothing.
He spoke, and they came hastening on to the steading.
Then Helios turned his horses toward the west,
bringing the evening day; and the fat flocks came up
from the pasture, climbing to the steadings and the folds.
And after them the cattle, countless, rank on rank,
came in sight like watery clouds,
such as move across the sky, driven onward
by the force of the south wind or the Thracian north;
of them as they go there is no number in the air,
nor any end; so many does the strength of the wind
roll on after the first, and others crest in turn behind the rest;
so many ever, behind the cattle, herd after herd came on.
And all the plain was filled, and all the paths,
with the wealth as it came (and the rich fields were straitened),
with lowing; and the byres were easily filled with the shambling
cattle, and the sheep settled down in the folds.
There no man, countless though they were,
stood idle by the cattle, lacking work;

title: Idylls
text:
but one fitted hobbles about their feet with well-cut thongs,
to milk them standing close around;
another set the dear young beneath their dear mothers
to drink, longing eagerly for the warm milk;
another held the milk-pail, another curdled the rich cheese,
another drove the bulls inside, apart from the heifers.
And Augeas went among all the cattle-byres,
to see what care his herdsmen took of his possessions,
and with him his son and the might of deep-thinking Heracles
walked beside the king as he passed through his great wealth.
Then, though he had a heart unbreakable in his breast,
and ever firmly fixed, the son of Amphitryon
marveled exceedingly at this countless gift of the gods
as he looked on. For no one would have said, or even hoped,
that one man's, or even ten others', flock could be so great,
even of all the kings who were richest in sheep.
But Helios gave his son this surpassing gift,
to be the richest in flocks of all men,
and he himself made all his cattle thrive ceaselessly
to the end; for no disease ever came upon his
herds, such as ruin the herdsmen's labors,
but ever more horned cattle, ever better,
year by year there came to be; for indeed all of them
brought forth living young, and bore females above measure.
And with them went three hundred bulls,
white-shanked and crook-horned, and two hundred others,
red; all these were already sires.
And besides these twelve more were grazing,
sacred to Helios; and in color they were like swans,
gleaming white, and they were preeminent among all the shambling cattle.
These grazed apart from the herd on the flourishing grass
in the pasture; so exceedingly proud were they of themselves.
And whenever from the thicket the swift wild beasts came out
into the plain after the cattle of the field,
these were the first to go to battle at the scent on the air,
and they bellowed dreadfully, with slaughter in their faces.
Among them in might and strength and overweening pride
stood out great Phaethon, whom the herdsmen
all likened to a star, because as he went among the other
cattle he shone bright, and was conspicuous.
And he, seeing the dry hide of the bright-eyed lion,
then charged at the keen-sighted Heracles himself,
to thrust his head and sturdy forehead against his ribs.
But the lord, as he came on, seized with his strong hand
his left horn at once, and bent his neck down to the ground
heavy though he was, and pushed him back again,
bearing down on his shoulder; and the muscle of the upper arm,
strained over the sinews, stood up upright.
And the lord himself marveled, and his warlike son
Phyleus, and the herdsmen by the crook-horned cattle,
seeing the overweening might of the son of Amphitryon.
Then the two, leaving there the rich fields,
set out for the city, Phyleus and the might of Heracles.
And they came first to the highway,
when they had finished a narrow path with their swift feet,
which ran through the vineyard from the steadings,
not very plain, threading green through the woodland;
and there the dear son of Augeas addressed
the offspring of Zeus most high, who walked behind him,
turning his head a little over his right shoulder:
Stranger, long ago I heard a certain tale about you,
if it is you, and I am now casting it about in my mind.
For there came a man, traveling from Argos in the prime of life,
an Achaean man, here from Helice by the sea,
who told us, among many of the Epeians,
that he had seen one of the Argives slay a beast,
a dread lion, an evil terror to the country folk,

title: Idylls
text:
that had its hollow lair by the grove of Zeus of Nemea;
I do not know exactly whether he was from holy Argos itself,
or dwelt in the city of Tiryns or Mycenae.
So that man told it; and he said his lineage,
if I rightly remember, was from Perseus.
I think no other of the men of Aegialus could have endured this
but you; and the beast's hide clearly proclaims
the strong work of your hands, that covers your sides.
Come, tell me first, that I may know in my heart,
hero, whether I divine truly or not,
whether you are that man of whom the Achaean from Helice
told us as we listened; and judge whether I mark you rightly.
And tell me how you yourself slew this deadly beast,
and how it came into the well-watered region of Nemea;
for you would not find so great a monster in Apis,
though you longed to see one, since it does not breed such great things,
but bears and boars and the deadly brood of wolves.
So we marveled then, hearing the tale;
and some said the wayfaring man was lying
to please those present with an idle tongue.
So saying, Phyleus turned aside from the middle of the road,
that as they went he might walk abreast,
and might more easily hear Heracles speak;
and falling in beside him he addressed him with such words:
Son of Augeas, what you first asked me,
you yourself have rightly judged by the line.
And about all the particulars of this monster
I will tell you, how they came to pass, since you long to hear,
except whence it came; for of all the many
Argives no one could tell it clearly;
only we guess that some one of the immortals,
angered over the sacrifices, sent it as a plague upon the sons of Phoroneus.
For like a river overflowing, the lion
ravaged all the Pisans without ceasing, and most of all the Bembinaeans,
who lived close to it, suffering unbearable things.
This labor Eurystheus laid on me to fulfill first,
and bade me slay the dread beast.
And I, taking my supple bow and the hollow quiver
full of arrows, set out, and in my other hand a club
well-jointed, with its own bark, of a spreading wild olive,
sound at the heart, which I myself, beneath holy Helicon,
having found it, tore up whole with its close-set roots.
But when I came to the place where the lion was,
then taking my bow I bent the twisted
string about the tip, and at once set on it an arrow charged with groans.
Turning my eyes everywhere I scanned for the deadly monster,
if I might catch sight of it before it saw me.
It was the middle of the day, and nowhere could I
mark its tracks, nor hear its roaring.
Nor was there any man to be seen with the cattle and the work
along the furrow of the sown field, whom I might ask;
but pale fear held every man at the steadings.
Yet I did not stay my feet, searching the long-leaved mountain,
before I saw it and at once made trial of my strength.
Indeed, toward evening it went to its lair,
gorged with flesh and blood; and its squalid mane
was spattered with gore, and its bright face
and breast, and with its tongue it licked round its chin.
But I quickly hid myself in the shady thickets
on the wooded ridge, watching where it should come,
and as it drew near I shot it in the left flank,
in vain; for the jagged arrow did not slip through the flesh,
but fell back upon the green grass.
And it suddenly raised its blood-red head from the ground
in amazement, and glared all around with its eyes,
peering, and gaping showed its greedy teeth.
And at it I sent another arrow from the string
in vexation, that the first had flown idly from my hand;

title: Idylls
text:
and in the middle of the breast I struck it, where the lung sits.
But not even so did the much-paining shaft sink beneath the hide,
but fell before its feet, all in vain.
A third time I was about, sorely grieved in my heart,
to draw the bow; but the relentless beast, glaring
round with its eyes, saw me, and curled its long tail
about its haunches, and at once bethought it of battle;
and all its neck was filled with rage, and its tawny mane
bristled with fury, and its spine arched like a bow,
drawn in all over at the flanks and the loins.
And as when a chariot-maker, skilled in many works,
bends the shoots of an easily split wild fig-tree,
heating them first in the fire, into wheels for an axled car,
and the thin-barked fig escapes from his hands
as it bends, and leaps far off at one bound;
so against me the dread lion from afar sprang in one rush,
eager to glut itself on my flesh; and I in my other
hand held out before me my darts and the doubled cloak from my shoulders,
and with the other, lifting the dry club above my temple,
I drove it down on its head, and broke clean in two
upon its very shaggy head the hard wild olive
of the irresistible beast; and it fell before it reached me
from on high to the ground, and stood on its trembling feet,
nodding its head; for darkness came over both its eyes,
the brain being shaken with violence in the bone.
And marking it as it was distracted with heavy pain,
before it could come to itself and breathe again,
I struck it first by the nape of its unbreakable neck,
throwing my bow to the ground and the well-stitched quiver;
and I throttled it mightily, pressing my strong hands
from behind, lest it should tear my flesh with its claws;
and against the ground I pressed its hind feet hard with my heels,
standing on them, and guarded its sides with my thighs,
until I stretched out its forelegs, lifting it upright,
breathless, and monstrous Hades received its soul.
And then I took thought how to strip the shaggy-necked hide
of the dead beast from its limbs,
a most grievous toil, since it could not be cut by iron
when I tried, nor by stones, nor by anything else.
Then one of the immortals put it in my mind to think
of cutting the lion's skin with its own claws.
With these I quickly flayed it, and put about my limbs
a guard against the flesh-cutting tumult of war.
This, my friend, was the slaying of the beast of Nemea,
that before had brought much grief to flocks and to men.
26. The Lenae, or Bacchantes
Ino and Autonoe and apple-cheeked Agave
led three companies to the mountain, three themselves.
And some, gathering the wild leaves of the shaggy oak
and living ivy and asphodel that grows above the ground,
wrought in a clean meadow twelve altars,
three to Semele, nine to Dionysus.
And taking from the basket the sacred cakes in their hands
they laid them reverently on the new-cut altars,
as he had taught, as Dionysus himself was well pleased.
But Pentheus watched it all from a sheer rock,
hidden in an old mastic-tree, a plant of the country.
Autonoe saw him first and cried out terribly,
and with her feet she scattered the rites of frenzied Bacchus,
rushing suddenly upon them, the rites that the profane may not see.
She herself went mad, and at once the others too went mad.
Pentheus fled in terror, and they pursued him,
drawing their robes from the girdle up to the knee.
Pentheus said this: What do you want, women?
Autonoe said this: You shall soon know, before you hear.
His mother seized her son's head and roared over it,

title: Idylls
text:
loud as the roar of a lioness over her cubs;
and Ino tore off the great shoulder with the shoulder-blade,
planting her heel upon his belly; and Autonoe's way was the same;
and the other women carved up what flesh was left.
And they came to Thebes all spattered with blood,
bringing from the mountain mourning, and not Pentheus.
I do not care; nor let any other take thought
for one hateful to Dionysus, not even if he had suffered worse than this,
were he a child of nine years, or just entering his tenth;
but let me be pure, and please those who are pure.
This honor the eagle has from Zeus, lord of the aegis.
To the children of the pious comes the better part, and not to the impious.
Hail, Dionysus, whom Zeus most high, on snowy Dracanon,
set in his great thigh, having loosed it open;
and hail, fair Semele, and her sisters,
the daughters of Cadmus, honored by many heroines,
who did this deed at the stirring of Dionysus,
a deed not to be blamed. Let no one find fault with the works of the gods.
27. The Lovers' Talk
Girl
Wise Helen was carried off by Paris, another cowherd.
Daphnis
Rather it was Helen who, of her own will, kissed the cowherd and kept him.
Girl
Do not boast, little satyr; an empty thing, they say, is a kiss.
Daphnis
Even in empty kisses there is a sweet delight.
Girl
I wash my mouth and spit away your kiss.
Daphnis
You wash your lips? Give them again, that I may kiss you.
Girl
It becomes you to kiss your heifers, not an unwedded girl.
Daphnis
Do not boast; for soon your youth passes by like a dream.
Girl
And if I grow somewhat old, I drink, no doubt, honey and milk for that.
Daphnis
. . .
Girl
The grape becomes a raisin, and the dried rose will not perish.
Daphnis
Come here, under the wild olives, that I may tell you a tale.
Girl
I will not; before now you beguiled me with a sweet tale.
Daphnis
Come here, under the elms, that you may hear my pipe.
Girl
Delight your own heart; nothing sad can please me.
Daphnis
Alas, alas, you too, girl, beware the wrath of the Paphian.
Girl
Farewell to the Paphian; only let Artemis be gracious to me.
Daphnis
Do not say it, lest she strike you and you fall into an inextricable net.
Girl
Let her strike as she will; Artemis again will help me.
Daphnis
You do not escape Love, whom no other maiden escaped.
Girl
I escape him, by Pan; but you ever bear his yoke.
Daphnis
I fear lest she give you to a worse man.
Girl
Many have wooed me, but none has won my heart.
Daphnis
I too come here, one of many, your suitor.
Girl
And what shall I do, friend? Marriages are full of troubles.
Daphnis
Marriage holds no pain, no grief, but dancing.
Girl
Yes, but they say women dread their husbands.
Daphnis
Rather they always rule them; whom do women dread?
Girl
I dread childbirth; harsh is the dart of Eileithyia.
Daphnis
But Artemis, your queen, eases the pangs of birth.
Girl
But I dread to bear a child, lest I lose my fair beauty too.
Daphnis
But if you bear dear children, you will see your sons as a new light.
Girl
And what wedding-gift do you bring me, worthy of marriage, if I consent?
Daphnis
All my herd you shall have, all the groves and the pasture.
Girl
Swear that you will not, when the wedding is done, leave me against my will and go.
Daphnis
By Pan himself, no, not even if you should wish to drive me off.
Girl
Will you build me bridal chambers, will you build a house and courtyards?
Daphnis
I will build you bridal chambers; and the fair flocks I tend.
Girl
But to my aged father, what tale shall I tell, what story?

title: Idylls
text:
Daphnis
He will approve your marriage, when he hears my name.
Girl
Tell me that name of yours; even a name often gives delight.
Daphnis
I am Daphnis, and Lycidas is my father, and my mother Nomaea.
Girl
You are of good birth; but I am no meaner than you.
Daphnis
I know, you are of the highest honor; and your father is Menalcas.
. . .
28. The Distaff
Distaff, friend of the spinner, gift of gray-eyed Athena
to women whose minds are set on the keeping of a thrifty house,
take heart and come with us to the bright city of Neleus,
where the precinct of Cypris is green beneath the soft reeds.
For there I ask of Zeus a voyage with fair winds,
that I may have the joy of seeing my friend and be loved in return,
Nicias, holy offshoot of the sweet-voiced Graces;
and you, born from ivory by much labor,
I will give as a gift into the hands of Nicias' wife,
with whom you shall accomplish much work for men's cloaks,
and much of the watery raiment that women wear.
For twice in the year the mothers of the lambs would have
their soft fleeces sheared in the pasture, for the sake of slender-ankled Theugenis;
so industrious is she, and loves all that the prudent love.
For I would not have wished to bring you to the house
of a slack or idle woman, you who are from our own land.
For your fatherland is the one that Archias once founded out of Ephyra,
the marrow of the Trinacrian isle, a city of noble men.
But now, dwelling in the house of a man who has learned much wise lore
to ward off baneful diseases from men,
you shall live in lovely Miletus among the Ionians,
that Theugenis may be renowned for her distaff among the townswomen,
and that you may ever keep for her the memory of her song-loving guest.
For seeing you a man will say this word: Great is the favor
with a small gift; and all that comes from friends is precious.
29. A Love-Poem
Wine, dear boy, they say, and truth go together;
and we too, being drunk, must be truthful.
And I will tell you what lies in the depth of my heart.
You do not wish to love me wholly, from your heart.
I know it; for I have half my life
through your beauty, but the rest is lost.
And when you are willing, I pass a day
like the blessed; but when you are unwilling, deep in darkness.
How is this fitting, to give the one who loves you pains?
But if you would take my word, the younger from the elder,
you would profit by it, and would praise me afterward:
make one nest in a single tree,
where no savage creeping thing will come.
But as it is, you hold one branch one day,
and another the next, and you seek one after another;
and if anyone, seeing your fair face, should praise it,
you become straightway more than a three years' friend to him,
while the one who first loved you, you reckon a friend of three days.
You seem to breathe the airs of overweening men.
But love, while still you may, one of your own kind always.
For if you do thus, you shall be well spoken of
among the townsmen, and Love will not be harsh to you,
Love who easily subdues the minds of men,
and made me soft out of iron.
But by your soft mouth I beseech you,
remember that last year you were younger,
and that we grow old before we can spit it away,
and wrinkled; and to have youth back again
is not possible, for it bears wings upon its shoulders,
and we are too slow to catch the things that fly.
Knowing this, you should be the kinder,
and love me, who love you, without guile,
so that, when you have a man's beard,
we may be to each other friends like Achilles and his comrade.

title: Idylls
text:
But if you give these words to the winds to carry off,
and say in your heart, Why, strange man, do you trouble me?
then now, even for golden apples, for your sake,
I would go, and to Cerberus, the warder of the dead;
but then, though you called me at the courtyard doors,
I would not come forth, having ceased from my cruel longing.
30. The Boy
Alas for this cruel and ill-fated sickness:
a quartan fever, love for a boy, holds me now a second month,
of beauty modest enough, yet as much as his feet rise
above the ground, that is grace; and on his cheeks there is a sweet smile.
And now the malady holds me some days, and other days no longer,
and soon there will not even be such respite as comes with sleep;
for yesterday, passing by, he glanced at me sidelong beneath his brows,
ashamed to look me in the face, and his skin reddened.
And love laid hold of my heart yet more,
and I went off home with a wound, and my heart bitten.
And much, calling in my own spirit, I reasoned with it:
Why do you do these things? What end will there be of your folly?
Do you not know that you carry white hairs at your temples?
It is time for you to be wise, not still young in your looks.
You do everything just like those who have only now tasted their years.
And another thing escapes you: it would have been far better
to be a stranger altogether to the cruel longings for a lovely boy.
For his life runs on, like the swift deer's, to forefathers gone,
and tomorrow he will spread his sails to cross another sea;
and the flower of sweet youth does not stay for him
among his comrades; but for me the longing eats even the marrow within,
as I remember; and many things I see in dreams at night,
and a year is not enough to end the cruel sickness.
These things and many others I reproached to my heart.
And it answered thus: Whoever thinks to conquer
the wily-scheming Love, let him think he can easily find
how many times nine are the stars above us.
And now, whether I will or no, I must stretch my long neck
and draw the yoke; for this, good sir,
is the will of the god, who overthrew even the great mind of Zeus
and of the Cyprus-born herself; and me, a leaf that lasts but a day,
needing only a small breath of wind, he carries where he will.
